In a DDP or FSDP job, this specific pattern, most ranks busy and a small minority idle, is the classic signature of one or more straggler ranks: because collective operations like all-reduce are synchronous, every rank must wait for the slowest rank to reach the collective before any of them can proceed, so GPUs 3 and 7 being idle most of the time doesn't mean they're doing less useful work, it means the other six GPUs are likely sitting in a blocked wait state for 3 and 7 to catch up, which would actually show up as lower effective utilization on the busy-looking GPUs too if you looked at a finer time resolution. What you cannot conclude from this alone is why ranks 3 and 7 are slow: it could be a hardware issue specific to those two GPUs (thermal throttling, an Xid error, ECC errors), a data-loading bottleneck specific to whatever shard those ranks are assigned, or a software-level issue like those two processes being scheduled on a NUMA node with worse CPU/memory locality for their data loader. The next steps are to check `nvidia-smi -q -d PERFORMANCE,CLOCK` or the system's Xid error logs for those two specific GPUs to rule out a hardware fault, check per-rank step timing logs (if instrumented) to confirm which ranks are actually slow versus which are waiting, and check whether ranks 3 and 7 happen to share a NUMA node, PCIe root complex, or data shard with some structural disadvantage.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing that jumps out immediately is GPUs 3 and 7 — they're sitting at about 22% sm utilization while everyone else is at 93-95%. In a DDP job that's the textbook straggler pattern: all-reduce is synchronous, so if two ranks are genuinely slower, the other six aren't actually doing 93% useful work either, they're mostly blocked waiting on 3 and 7 to reach the next collective — nvidia-smi just can't tell you that distinction, it only shows device-wide utilization sampled over time, not 'busy computing' versus 'busy waiting in a collective.' What I can't tell from this snapshot alone is why 3 and 7 are slow. Next steps, in order of cheapest-first: check for Xid errors or thermal throttling specifically on those two GPUs, since a hardware fault or thermal issue is a common, boring explanation; check whether per-rank step timing logs (if the job logs them) actually confirm 3 and 7 are the ones lagging rather than it being some artifact of sampling timing; and check whether those two ranks happen to share a NUMA node or a slower PCIe path that's giving their data loaders worse throughput than the other six. I wouldn't jump to 'the network is bad' or 'the model code is slow' from this output alone — this points specifically at two individual GPUs, not the fabric or the model.
commonMistakes: Concluding the two low-utilization GPUs are simply doing less work, without considering they might be causing the other six to wait
Treating nvidia-smi dmon's device-wide sampling as equivalent to per-kernel or per-rank diagnostic detail
Jumping to a network/fabric explanation when the symptom is isolated to two specific GPUs, not a general slowdown
Not checking hardware-level signals (Xid errors, thermal throttling) for the two specific underperforming GPUs first
Assuming high sm% on the other six GPUs definitely means they're doing useful compute rather than spin-waiting on a collective
keyPoints: sm/mem utilization is device-wide and time-sampled, not per-kernel or per-rank detail
Two low-utilization GPUs among otherwise-busy peers in a DDP job is the classic straggler signature
Synchronous collectives mean the 'busy' GPUs may actually be blocked waiting on the stragglers
This output alone cannot identify the straggler's root cause (hardware, data, NUMA locality)
Next steps: check Xid/thermal logs, per-rank timing, and NUMA/PCIe locality for the specific underperforming GPUs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the straggler pattern from the utilization numbers
Correctly explains why busy-looking GPUs may actually be blocked waiting
Correctly states what cannot be concluded from this data alone
Proposes concrete, sensibly ordered next diagnostic steps

questions.title: Diagnose a DCGM Metric Signature for a Communication-Bound Step
questions.prompt: Your monitoring dashboard for a distributed training job shows the DCGM metrics below, sustained for the duration of a step. Interpret this specific combination and explain what it does and doesn't tell you about where the bottleneck actually is.
questions.code:
DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL:            98%
DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE: 11%
DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_ACTIVE:        24%
DCGM_FI_PROF_NVLINK_TX_BYTES:    very high, sustained
questions.modelAnswer: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL only reports whether some kernel was running on the GPU at all during the sampling window; it's a 'was something busy' signal, not a 'was it doing useful tensor-core math' signal. DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE is the much closer proxy for actual tensor-core compute efficiency, and here it's at 11%, far below the 98% GPU_UTIL figure, which is the specific fingerprint of a GPU that looks fully busy while doing very little real matrix-multiplication work. DRAM_ACTIVE at 24% rules out this being a classic memory-bound kernel pattern (where DRAM activity would typically be high while tensor activity is low), which combined with sustained, high NVLink TX byte throughput points instead at the GPU spending most of its time moving data over NVLink, i.e., this step is communication-bound, consistent with a collective operation (all-reduce, all-gather, or reduce-scatter) dominating the step rather than a data-loading stall or a genuinely slow matmul kernel. What this specific combination tells you is that the bottleneck for this step is almost certainly inter-GPU communication, not compute and not storage/data-loading (which would more likely show up as low GPU_UTIL overall, GPUs sitting idle waiting for a batch, rather than high GPU_UTIL with low tensor activity and high NVLink traffic). What it does not tell you is which specific collective, at which point in the model (gradient sync after backward, versus an FSDP all-gather of parameters before a forward/backward), is responsible, or whether the communication volume itself is excessive relative to what's necessary versus the fabric being undersized for a reasonable volume; that requires either Nsight Systems' timeline view to see which NCCL call dominates the step, or nccl-tests run in isolation to establish whether the fabric itself is underperforming its rated bandwidth.
questions.professionalAnswer: The read here is: GPU_UTIL at 98% but PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE at only 11% is exactly the signature people get tricked by all the time — the GPU looks maxed out on a dashboard, but it's not actually doing much real matrix-multiplication work. DRAM_ACTIVE being low too (24%) tells me this isn't the usual memory-bound story either, where you'd expect DRAM traffic to be high instead. What ties it together is the NVLink TX byte counter being sustained and high — that points squarely at this step being dominated by inter-GPU communication, most likely a collective like all-reduce or an FSDP all-gather, not compute and not a data-loading stall. What I can't tell from these four numbers alone is which specific collective call is eating the time, or whether the actual data volume being moved is reasonable but the fabric's underperforming, versus the volume itself being unnecessarily large for what the model actually needs to synchronize. For that I'd pull up an Nsight Systems timeline to see exactly which NCCL call is dominating the step, and separately run nccl-tests in isolation to confirm whether the fabric itself is hitting its rated busbw or underperforming it.
commonMistakes: Treating high GPU_UTIL alone as evidence the GPU is doing useful compute work
Not recognizing PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE as the more reliable proxy for tensor-core compute efficiency
Confusing this communication-bound signature with a classic memory-bound (high DRAM_ACTIVE) kernel pattern
Concluding the exact root cause (which collective, insufficient fabric vs. excessive volume) from these metrics alone
Jumping straight to 'buy a faster network' before confirming with Nsight Systems or nccl-tests what's actually dominating
keyPoints: GPU_UTIL answers only whether a kernel was running, not whether it was doing useful compute
PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE is the closer proxy for real tensor-core efficiency; it's low here despite high GPU_UTIL
Low DRAM_ACTIVE rules out the classic memory-bound signature
High, sustained NVLink TX throughput points at a communication-bound step, likely a collective operation
Confirming which specific collective and whether the fabric is underperforming requires Nsight Systems or nccl-tests, not DCGM alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reads the high-GPU_UTIL/low-PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE signature
Correctly rules out the memory-bound pattern using DRAM_ACTIVE
Correctly connects high NVLink throughput to a communication-bound diagnosis
Correctly states the limits of what these metrics alone can tell you

questions.title: Fix a Kubernetes GPU Pod Spec Stuck Pending
questions.prompt: This Pod spec has been stuck in Pending for 20 minutes. `kubectl describe pod` shows a FailedScheduling event: '0/12 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu.' The cluster has 4 nodes with 8 free A100s each and 8 nodes with no GPUs at all. Diagnose the likely cause and fix the spec.
questions.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: training-worker
spec:
  containers:
    - name: trainer
      image: registry.internal/trainer:latest
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 1
        requests:
          cpu: "4"
          memory: "16Gi"
questions.modelAnswer: The event '0/12 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' means the scheduler evaluated all 12 nodes and found none satisfying the GPU resource request, which initially sounds like a contradiction given 4 nodes report 8 free A100s each. The most common concrete cause of this exact symptom with otherwise-correct resources.limits is that the NVIDIA device plugin DaemonSet either isn't running, has crashed, or hasn't fully initialized on the 4 GPU nodes, so those nodes' allocatable resource list never actually advertises nvidia.com/gpu capacity to the scheduler even though nvidia-smi on the node itself would show the GPUs as physically present and idle; from the scheduler's point of view, a node that doesn't advertise the resource in its Allocatable list is indistinguishable from a node that has none. The spec itself is not the bug here (requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 in limits only, with no corresponding request, is actually the standard, correct pattern for GPU resources, which don't support fractional allocation and don't need a separate request field the way CPU/memory do). The fix is operational, not a change to this YAML: check kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l name=nvidia-device-plugin-ds (or whatever the plugin DaemonSet is labeled) to confirm it's Running and not CrashLoopBackOff on the 4 GPU nodes, and check kubectl describe node <gpu-node> for an Allocatable block that actually lists nvidia.com/gpu: 8; if the plugin is down, restarting it (or fixing whatever caused its crash, often a driver/plugin version mismatch) is what resolves the Pending state, not any change to the Pod spec.
questions.professionalAnswer: The spec itself is actually fine — nvidia.com/gpu: 1 in limits with no separate request is the normal, correct pattern since GPU resources aren't fractionally divisible the way CPU is. What's suspicious is the scheduler saying all 12 nodes, including the 4 with GPUs, have insufficient nvidia.com/gpu — if the GPUs were physically there and advertised correctly, you'd expect a different error on at least the GPU nodes. My first move would be checking the NVIDIA device plugin DaemonSet, because this exact symptom — physically-present GPUs the scheduler claims aren't there — is almost always the plugin not running or not having registered the resource with the node yet. I'd run kubectl get pods -n kube-system to check the plugin's status on those 4 nodes, and kubectl describe node on one of them to see whether Allocatable actually lists nvidia.com/gpu at all. If the plugin's crashed or never started, that's an operational fix — restart it, check for a driver-version mismatch against the plugin's expected CUDA driver version — not something you fix by editing this Pod YAML, since the YAML is asking for exactly what it should be asking for.
questions.example: kubectl describe node gpu-node-1 shows Capacity: nvidia.com/gpu: 8 but Allocatable: nvidia.com/gpu: 0 — the device plugin advertised the physical GPU count once at node registration but a later crash left Allocatable at zero, which is exactly what produces this FailedScheduling event despite GPUs being physically idle.
commonMistakes: Assuming the Pod spec itself must be wrong when the resource request syntax is actually standard and correct
Not checking the device plugin DaemonSet's health as the first diagnostic step for this specific error message
Confusing Capacity (what the node physically has) with Allocatable (what the scheduler actually sees as available)
Trying to fix a device-plugin problem by modifying resource requests/limits in the Pod spec
Not checking for a driver-version mismatch between the node's NVIDIA driver and the device plugin's expectations
keyPoints: The Pod spec's resource syntax (limits-only nvidia.com/gpu) is already correct, not the bug
'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' across GPU nodes despite physical availability points to the device plugin
Allocatable, not Capacity, is what the scheduler actually checks
The fix is operational (restart/repair the device plugin DaemonSet), not a YAML change
A driver/plugin version mismatch is a common root cause of the plugin failing to register the resource

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recognizes the Pod spec's resource syntax is not the actual bug
Correctly diagnoses the device plugin as the likely root cause
Correctly distinguishes Capacity from Allocatable
Names concrete diagnostic commands/checks

questions.title: Fix a torchrun Elastic Launch That Never Reaches the Required Minimum Nodes
questions.prompt: This torchrun elastic launch command is intended to run on anywhere from 4 to 16 nodes, but the job keeps timing out at rendezvous with only 3 nodes having joined, even though 10 nodes attempted to launch. Identify the bug in the command and correct it.
questions.modelAnswer: The command itself is actually well-formed for a straightforward elastic launch, which means the described symptom (only 3 of 10 attempting nodes actually joining rendezvous) points at a problem outside this specific command's syntax: the rdzv_endpoint, 10.0.0.5:29500, must be reachable from every participating node, and if 10.0.0.5 is one specific node's own address (rather than a stable, shared rendezvous point reachable by all nodes, such as a load-balanced or otherwise consistently-addressed service), any node that cannot route to that exact IP on that port will fail to join rendezvous, which would produce exactly this symptom: some nodes (those with a network path to 10.0.0.5) join, others silently fail to reach it and time out separately. In practice, for jobs orchestrated by Kubernetes (e.g., via the Kubeflow Training Operator's PyTorchJob), the fix is to use the rendezvous address the orchestrator injects (commonly exposed as an environment variable like PET_MASTER_ADDR or a Kubernetes Service DNS name for the designated rendezvous node) rather than a hardcoded IP, since a hardcoded address is both fragile (it breaks if that node is rescheduled to a different IP) and, if it's not actually reachable from every node due to network policy or the node simply not existing at that address anymore, explains precisely why most attempting nodes fail to join while a minority succeed. The corrected invocation should reference a stable, cluster-resolvable rendezvous address, for example --rdzv_endpoint=$PET_MASTER_ADDR:29500 or a Kubernetes headless Service DNS name, rather than a literal IP that may not be uniformly reachable or may have changed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The flags themselves — nnodes=4:16, nproc_per_node=8, rdzv_backend=c10d — are all reasonable for an elastic job. The thing I'd actually suspect given the symptom is the hardcoded rdzv_endpoint, 10.0.0.5:29500. If that's a specific node's IP rather than a stable, shared address every node can actually reach, you get exactly this failure pattern — some nodes happen to have a network path to that address and join fine, others can't reach it at all (maybe it's not even the right node anymore if there was a reschedule) and just silently time out trying. I'd swap the hardcoded IP for whatever stable rendezvous address the orchestrator actually provides — in a Kubernetes/Kubeflow setup that's usually an injected environment variable or a headless Service DNS name that resolves consistently regardless of which physical node ends up hosting it. Hardcoding a literal IP for the rendezvous endpoint is fragile in exactly the way this symptom shows: it works for whichever nodes happen to have a path to that address, and silently fails for the rest, which looks like 'some nodes joined, most didn't' rather than a clean, obvious error.
questions.example: --rdzv_endpoint=$PET_MASTER_ADDR:29500 using an environment variable the orchestrator sets to a stable, resolvable rendezvous host, instead of --rdzv_endpoint=10.0.0.5:29500 hardcoded to one specific node's IP that may be unreachable from other nodes or may no longer be the intended rendezvous host.
commonMistakes: Assuming the --nnodes range or --max-restarts value is the bug when the real issue is network reachability
Hardcoding a literal IP address for rdzv_endpoint instead of a stable, orchestrator-provided address
Not recognizing that partial, inconsistent join behavior across nodes points at a reachability problem rather than a syntax error
Confusing rendezvous timeout (nodes can't find each other) with a resource-availability timeout (not enough nodes exist)
Not checking whether the rendezvous endpoint's node was rescheduled to a different IP since the command was last correct
keyPoints: The torchrun flags themselves are syntactically correct for an elastic launch
A hardcoded rdzv_endpoint IP that isn't uniformly reachable produces exactly this partial-join symptom
Only nodes with a network path to that specific IP succeed; others silently time out
The fix is using a stable, cluster-resolvable rendezvous address (env var or Service DNS) instead of a literal IP
This is a reachability/addressing problem, not a flag-syntax problem

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that the command's flags are not the actual bug
Correctly diagnoses the hardcoded rdzv_endpoint as the root cause
Explains why this produces a partial-join pattern specifically
Proposes a correct, stable fix

questions.title: Fix a Volcano PodGroup That Allows Partial Scheduling
questions.prompt: This Volcano PodGroup is meant to gang-schedule a 64-pod training job so all pods start together or none do, but the cluster has started 40 of the 64 pods while the other 24 stay Pending, and the 40 running pods are failing because rendezvous never completes. Find the configuration bug and fix it.
questions.code:
apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1
kind: PodGroup
metadata:
  name: training-job-4471
spec:
  minMember: 1
  queue: language-modeling
  minResources:
    cpu: "256"
    memory: "2048Gi"
    nvidia.com/gpu: "64"
questions.modelAnswer: minMember: 1 is the bug. minMember is the field that actually enforces Volcano's all-or-nothing gang-scheduling guarantee: it tells the scheduler the minimum number of pods in this group that must be schedulable together before any of them are placed. With it set to 1, Volcano's gang constraint is satisfied as soon as a single pod can be scheduled, which defeats the entire purpose of using a PodGroup for this job: the scheduler is free to place pods incrementally as capacity becomes available rather than waiting for all 64 to be placeable at once, which is exactly why 40 pods started while 24 remained pending, a result indistinguishable from what plain, non-gang-scheduled Kubernetes scheduling would have produced. This matters specifically for a PyTorchJob-style training job because torchrun's rendezvous blocks until every expected rank joins, so a partial launch of 40 out of 64 expected ranks will never complete rendezvous and will eventually time out, burning GPU-hours on 40 nodes that can never actually start training. minResources is correctly set to reflect the full job's resource needs (256 CPU, 2048Gi memory, 64 GPUs), so that part of the spec is not the issue; the fix is setting minMember: 64 (matching the actual number of pods in the job) so Volcano holds every pod Pending until all 64 can be scheduled together, and only then releases the entire group at once.
questions.professionalAnswer: minMember: 1 is exactly backwards for what this job needs. That field is Volcano's actual gang-scheduling guarantee — it's the number of pods that have to be simultaneously schedulable before any of them get placed — and setting it to 1 means the gang constraint is trivially satisfied the moment even one pod can be scheduled, so Volcano behaves basically like plain Kubernetes scheduling pods incrementally as capacity frees up. That's precisely the symptom described: 40 pods started, 24 didn't, and because torchrun's rendezvous blocks waiting for every one of the 64 expected ranks to join, those 40 running pods are stuck forever, burning GPU-hours on a job that structurally can't start. minResources looks right — it matches the full job's footprint — so the fix is just changing minMember to 64, matching the actual pod count, so Volcano genuinely holds the whole group Pending until there's room for all 64 at once, then releases them together. I'd also double-check this against whatever templating or Helm chart generated this PodGroup, since a minMember default of 1 is an easy copy-paste mistake to carry forward from a different, non-gang-scheduled workload.
questions.example: minMember: 64 ensures Volcano only releases pods from this PodGroup once 64 pods can be scheduled simultaneously; with minResources already correctly sized for the full job, this guarantees the all-or-nothing behavior the job actually needs.
commonMistakes: Assuming minResources being correct means the whole spec is correct
Not recognizing minMember as the specific field enforcing the all-or-nothing gang guarantee
Treating a minMember value lower than the actual pod count as a harmless default rather than a functional bug
Missing the causal link between partial gang scheduling and torchrun's rendezvous blocking behavior
Fixing the symptom (killing the 40 stuck pods) without fixing the configuration that will reproduce it on the next launch
keyPoints: minMember, not minResources, is the field enforcing all-or-nothing gang scheduling
minMember: 1 trivially satisfies the gang constraint, allowing partial scheduling
This degrades to effectively ordinary incremental Kubernetes scheduling for this job
torchrun's rendezvous blocking means a partial launch wastes GPU-hours on pods that can never start
The fix is setting minMember to match the actual total pod count (64)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies minMember as the field controlling gang-scheduling behavior
Correctly diagnoses minMember: 1 as the specific bug
Connects the bug to the observed rendezvous-timeout symptom
Produces the correct fix

questions.title: Fix a Checkpoint-Resharding Mismatch With torch.distributed.checkpoint
questions.prompt: A training job checkpointed successfully on 32 GPUs under FSDP. Resuming the same run on 64 GPUs (a planned scale-up) fails during checkpoint load with a shape/metadata mismatch error. The team assumed torch.distributed.checkpoint (DCP) supports this automatically. Explain what's actually going wrong and how to fix the resume.
questions.modelAnswer: DCP genuinely does support resharding onto a different number of ranks, so the resharding capability itself is not the problem; the bug is in how dcp.load is being called. DCP's load works by reading the checkpoint's saved shard metadata and reshaping it onto whatever sharded state_dict structure you hand it, which means the state_dict passed into dcp.load must already be constructed from the model and optimizer as they exist under the new 64-GPU FSDP configuration (with FSDP's own sharding applied at that new world size) before the load call populates it; dcp.load fills in the values of an existing, correctly-shaped sharded state_dict, it does not conjure a correctly-shaped state_dict out of nothing. If the model and optimizer on the 64-GPU side were constructed identically in shape to the code above with no indication they're aware of the new world size, the most likely actual bug is that the model wasn't wrapped in FSDP (or was wrapped with different sharding configuration) before state_dict() was called to build the destination dict, so the shapes DCP is trying to reshard into don't match what DCP expects to find at a 64-rank sharding layout. The fix is ensuring the model is fully constructed and wrapped with FSDP under the new 64-GPU process group before calling model.state_dict() to build the destination state_dict, so that destination state_dict has the correct per-rank shard shapes for 64 GPUs, and only then calling dcp.load(state_dict, checkpoint_id=...) to have DCP read the 32-GPU-sharded checkpoint and correctly reshard its contents into that already-correctly-shaped 64-GPU destination.
questions.professionalAnswer: The resharding feature itself is real — DCP is built to let you save on N ranks and load on M ranks, so that's not the actual bug here. What's almost certainly wrong is the order of operations on the load side: dcp.load doesn't create a correctly-shaped sharded state_dict for you, it fills in values into a state_dict you've already built from your model as it exists right now, under whatever FSDP configuration is active at that moment. So if the model on the 64-GPU side wasn't actually constructed and wrapped in FSDP under the new 64-way process group before you called model.state_dict() to build the destination dict, you're handing dcp.load() a destination shape that doesn't match what it's expecting to reshard the 32-GPU checkpoint into, and that's exactly the shape/metadata mismatch you'd see. The fix is making sure the full model-construction-and-FSDP-wrap sequence happens under the new 64-GPU setup first, build the destination state_dict from that, and only then call dcp.load — DCP's resharding logic is reading the saved checkpoint's shard metadata and mapping it onto whatever shape you've already prepared, not inventing the right shape itself.
questions.example: model = GPT(config); model = FSDP(model, process_group=new_64gpu_pg); state_dict = {'model': model.state_dict(), 'optim': optimizer.state_dict()}; dcp.load(state_dict, checkpoint_id='ckpt/step-048000') -- the FSDP wrap under the new 64-GPU process group must happen before state_dict() is called, not after.
commonMistakes: Assuming DCP's resharding feature doesn't exist and reverting to a from-scratch training run instead of debugging the load call
Not realizing dcp.load fills an already-shaped destination state_dict rather than constructing one from the checkpoint
Constructing or wrapping the model under the new world size after, rather than before, building the destination state_dict
Assuming the error message's 'shape mismatch' refers to the checkpoint being corrupt rather than a load-side construction order problem
Not verifying the new process group / FSDP configuration actually reflects 64 ranks before calling state_dict()
keyPoints: DCP genuinely supports resharding checkpoints across different GPU counts
dcp.load fills values into an already-constructed, correctly-shaped destination state_dict; it doesn't create one
The destination state_dict must come from a model already wrapped in FSDP under the new (64-GPU) process group
Building that destination state_dict before fully constructing/wrapping the model under the new world size causes the mismatch
The fix is ordering: construct model, wrap in FSDP at new world size, call state_dict(), then dcp.load

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly affirms DCP genuinely supports resharding (not the actual bug)
Correctly explains that dcp.load fills a pre-shaped destination state_dict
Correctly identifies the construction-order bug on the 64-GPU side
Produces a correct fix with proper ordering

questions.title: Right-Size vLLM Startup Flags for a Memory-Constrained Deployment
questions.prompt: A vLLM server for a 13B model on a single 40GB GPU keeps hitting out-of-memory errors at startup, before any requests even arrive. The team's current launch command is below. Diagnose the likely misconfiguration and correct it so the server starts reliably with a reasonable KV cache budget.
questions.modelAnswer: Two choices in this command are driving the OOM, and both are worth fixing rather than just one. First, --dtype float32 forces the model's weights (and typically activations) into full 32-bit precision, which for a 13B-parameter model requires roughly 52GB just for weights before any KV cache is allocated at all, already exceeding a 40GB GPU; essentially no production vLLM deployment should run float32 for serving, bf16 or fp16 is the standard choice, cutting that weight footprint roughly in half to about 26GB, which actually fits. Second, --max-model-len 32768 sets the maximum context length vLLM must reserve KV cache capacity for, and combined with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 (instructing vLLM to try to use 95% of the GPU's memory for weights plus KV cache), a very long max context length multiplies the per-sequence KV cache reservation vLLM is trying to fit into whatever memory remains after loading the weights; if the actual workload doesn't need 32K-token contexts, lowering max-model-len to a value that matches real traffic (e.g. 8192 or 4096) frees substantially more memory for the KV cache without changing precision. The corrected command should use --dtype bfloat16 (or float16) as the primary fix, since that alone resolves the dominant weight-memory problem, and should also right-size --max-model-len to match actual expected request lengths rather than defaulting to the model's maximum supported context, with --gpu-memory-utilization left at a slightly more conservative value like 0.90 to leave headroom for CUDA's own overhead and avoid cutting it so close that a transient allocation spike still OOMs.
questions.professionalAnswer: The dtype flag is the big one here — float32 on a 13B model is roughly 52GB of weights alone, and that's already more than the 40GB GPU has before vLLM even tries to reserve KV cache space. Production LLM serving essentially never uses float32; bf16 or fp16 cuts that weight footprint to around 26GB, which actually fits with real room left over. The second thing I'd fix is max-model-len — 32768 reserves KV cache capacity sized for 32K-token sequences, and if the actual traffic doesn't need contexts anywhere near that long, that's memory being reserved for a scenario that isn't happening, crowding out the capacity you'd rather have for more concurrent requests at realistic lengths. I'd change --dtype to bfloat16 first since that alone probably gets the server past the OOM, then right-size max-model-len to whatever the real workload's p99 context length actually is rather than the model's architectural maximum, and I'd back gpu-memory-utilization down slightly to something like 0.90 so there's a bit of headroom for CUDA's own allocator overhead instead of trying to squeeze every last percent.
questions.example: vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-2-13b-hf --max-model-len 8192 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --dtype bfloat16 — weights now fit in roughly 26GB, leaving meaningful headroom on a 40GB GPU for a reasonably sized KV cache at a realistic context length.
commonMistakes: Only addressing gpu-memory-utilization without noticing float32 is the dominant cause of the memory footprint
Assuming higher gpu-memory-utilization values are always safe regardless of dtype or max-model-len
Setting max-model-len to the model's architectural maximum instead of the actual workload's real context lengths
Not recognizing that fp32 roughly doubles the weight memory footprint versus bf16/fp16
Leaving gpu-memory-utilization at a value so aggressive (0.95+) that any transient overhead still triggers an OOM
keyPoints: float32 weights for a 13B model require roughly 52GB, already exceeding the GPU before KV cache
bf16/fp16 cuts weight memory roughly in half, making the deployment fit
max-model-len should match real workload context lengths, not the model's architectural maximum
gpu-memory-utilization should leave some headroom below 1.0 for allocator overhead
Precision is the dominant lever here; context length is the secondary one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies float32 as the dominant cause of the OOM
Correctly explains max-model-len's effect on KV cache reservation
Produces a correct, reasonable corrected configuration
Addresses gpu-memory-utilization headroom sensibly

questions.title: Fix a Slurm Job Script That Launches Only One Process Per Node
questions.prompt: This Slurm batch script is meant to launch an 8-GPU-per-node, 4-node distributed training job (32 processes total), but logs show only 4 processes started, one per node, and the job fails immediately with a world-size mismatch. Find the bug and fix the script.
questions.modelAnswer: The sbatch directives are missing --ntasks-per-node (or an equivalent --ntasks setting), so Slurm's default of one task per node applies: srun launches exactly one task per node (4 total) regardless of what --nproc_per_node=8 tells torchrun to do within each task, because that default is determined by Slurm's own task allocation, not by any flag passed to torchrun. Each of those 4 srun-launched tasks then runs its own torchrun --nnodes=4 --nproc_per_node=8 command, but since there's only one such process per node rather than srun coordinating 8 tasks per node, you don't get the intended 32 total ranks; you get 4 separate single-task invocations each individually trying (and likely failing in some other way, or producing the world-size mismatch described) to run an 8-process-per-node torchrun setup from inside a context where Slurm only ever started one task. Also, $SLURM_NODELIST is a compressed node-list string (e.g., node[01-04]) rather than a single resolvable hostname, which is a second, independent bug: the rendezvous endpoint needs one specific, resolvable host:port, not a list. The fixes are adding #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1 explicitly if the intent is one torchrun launcher per node (each spawning its own 8 processes via --nproc_per_node, which is actually the standard correct pattern, so the ntasks-per-node=1 default accidentally matches the intent here) combined with fixing rdzv_endpoint to reference a single resolvable master node, typically obtained via a helper like $(scontrol show hostnames $SLURM_NODELIST | head -n 1):29500 rather than the raw, compressed $SLURM_NODELIST variable.
questions.professionalAnswer: There are actually two separate bugs stacked here. The one causing the immediate world-size mismatch is rdzv_endpoint — $SLURM_NODELIST isn't a single resolvable host, it's Slurm's compressed node-list notation like node[01-04], and torchrun needs one specific host:port for rendezvous, not a list string. That alone would break rendezvous regardless of the task-count issue. The second thing worth checking, even though in this specific pattern it happens to be correct by coincidence, is that one srun task per node, each running torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 to spawn its own 8 processes locally, is actually the standard, correct way to do this — Slurm's default of one task per node is fine here because torchrun itself is responsible for fanning out to 8 local processes, srun doesn't need to launch 8 tasks per node for that. So the real fix is just resolving rdzv_endpoint to a single actual hostname — something like $(scontrol show hostnames $SLURM_NODELIST | head -n 1):29500 — rather than passing the raw, compressed node-list variable straight through. I'd double check the logs again after that fix to confirm it really is 4 torchrun launchers (one per node) each correctly spawning 8 local processes, giving the intended 32 total ranks.
questions.example: MASTER_NODE=$(scontrol show hostnames $SLURM_NODELIST | head -n 1); srun torchrun --nnodes=4 --nproc_per_node=8 --rdzv_id=$SLURM_JOB_ID --rdzv_backend=c10d --rdzv_endpoint=$MASTER_NODE:29500 train.py — resolves SLURM_NODELIST's compressed notation into one real hostname before using it as the rendezvous endpoint.
commonMistakes: Assuming --nproc_per_node alone controls how many Slurm tasks are launched per node
Passing $SLURM_NODELIST directly as a hostname without resolving its compressed node-list notation
Adding an unnecessary --ntasks-per-node=8, which would actually launch 8 redundant torchrun invocations per node instead of one that correctly fans out to 8 local processes
Not distinguishing a rendezvous/addressing bug from a Slurm task-allocation bug when both can produce similar-looking symptoms
Forgetting that srun's default task-per-node count depends on sbatch directives, not on flags passed to the program it launches
keyPoints: srun's default of one task per node is actually correct here, since torchrun itself fans out to 8 local processes via --nproc_per_node
The real bug is $SLURM_NODELIST being a compressed node-list notation, not a single resolvable hostname
rdzv_endpoint needs one specific, resolvable host:port for rendezvous to succeed
scontrol show hostnames is the standard way to resolve SLURM_NODELIST into actual hostnames
Misreading this as a task-count problem rather than an addressing problem would lead to an unnecessary, incorrect fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the SLURM_NODELIST addressing bug as the real root cause
Correctly explains why one srun task per node is actually the intended, correct pattern here
Produces a correct fix resolving the node list to a single hostname
Does not introduce an incorrect ntasks-per-node change

questions.title: Interpret nccl-tests Output to Diagnose a Fabric Problem
questions.prompt: You run nccl-tests' all_reduce_perf benchmark in isolation (no training job running) across 16 nodes connected by a fabric rated for 400 Gb/s per port. The output below shows the result for the largest message size tested. Determine whether the fabric is performing acceptably and what you'd check next.
questions.code:
#     size   count   type   redop   time    algbw   busbw  #wrong
# (B)   (elements)             (us)   (GB/s)  (GB/s)
536870912  134217728  float    sum    68421    7.85    14.72       0
questions.modelAnswer: The number to compare against the fabric's rated hardware bandwidth is busbw (14.72 GB/s), not algbw (7.85 GB/s), because busbw already accounts for the ring all-reduce communication factor 2(N-1)/N, which is what makes it comparable to a link's actual rated bandwidth, whereas algbw is just message-size-over-time and systematically understates real data movement across the wire. Converting the fabric's rating to comparable units: 400 Gb/s is 50 GB/s (dividing by 8), so a busbw of 14.72 GB/s represents only about 29% of the rated 400 Gb/s fabric's capacity, which is a significant shortfall, not a healthy result; a well-performing InfiniBand or equivalent fabric at this scale would typically be expected to sustain a much higher fraction of its rated bandwidth for a large all-reduce. This gap points at a real fabric health problem rather than an inherent limitation of all-reduce at 16 nodes, since 16 nodes is not large enough for the (N-1)/N factor alone to explain this much shortfall. The next steps are checking each node's InfiniBand port counters with ibstat and perfquery for signs of a degraded link (lower negotiated speed than expected) or a climbing CRC/symbol error count, checking whether all 16 nodes are actually using the fabric's fastest available path (e.g., confirming via NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs that NCCL selected the InfiniBand/RDMA transport rather than silently falling back to a slower TCP/Ethernet path for some reason), and checking whether the switch topology has an oversubscription bottleneck that caps achievable bisection bandwidth below the per-port rating.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing: compare busbw, not algbw, against the rated fabric speed — busbw already folds in the ring all-reduce communication factor, so it's the number that's actually comparable to a link's rated bandwidth. 400 Gb/s converts to 50 GB/s, and a busbw of 14.72 GB/s is only about 29% of that — that's not a healthy number, a fabric performing well at this scale should be sustaining a lot more of its rated capacity on a large all-reduce. I wouldn't chalk this up to 'that's just how all-reduce scales' either — 16 nodes isn't large enough for the (N-1)/N factor to explain a shortfall this big on its own. My next steps: pull ibstat and perfquery on each node to check for a degraded link speed or a climbing CRC error count, which is a classic 'physically fine but underperforming' signature; turn on NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and confirm NCCL is actually using the InfiniBand/RDMA transport and hasn't silently fallen back to something slower; and check the switch fabric's actual topology for an oversubscription ratio that caps bisection bandwidth below what the per-port rating alone would suggest.
commonMistakes: Comparing algbw instead of busbw against the fabric's rated bandwidth
Forgetting to convert Gb/s to GB/s (dividing by 8) before comparing against busbw
Attributing a large shortfall entirely to the expected (N-1)/N ring all-reduce scaling factor at a node count too small to explain it
Not checking whether NCCL actually selected the fast transport rather than silently falling back to a slower one
Jumping straight to a hardware replacement decision before checking port counters, transport selection, and topology
keyPoints: busbw, not algbw, is the number comparable to a fabric's rated hardware bandwidth
400 Gb/s converts to 50 GB/s; 14.72 GB/s busbw is only about 29% of that rating
16 nodes is not large enough for ring all-reduce's (N-1)/N factor alone to explain this shortfall
Next checks: ibstat/perfquery for link degradation or CRC errors, NCCL_DEBUG=INFO for transport selection, switch oversubscription
This is a real fabric-health signal worth investigating, not an expected scaling artifact

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies busbw as the metric to compare against rated bandwidth
Correctly performs the Gb/s-to-GB/s conversion and the resulting percentage assessment
Correctly concludes this is a real shortfall, not expected scaling behavior
Proposes concrete, sensible next diagnostic steps

questions.title: Diagnose a Data Loader Bottleneck From Training Loop Behavior
questions.prompt: A training job's GPUs show CPU and GPU both under-utilized at the same time, with a visible gap in the profiler trace between when a batch is ready on CPU and when it's visible to the GPU. The current DataLoader configuration is below. Diagnose the likely cause and propose a fix.
questions.code:
train_loader = DataLoader(
    dataset,
    batch_size=256,
    shuffle=True,
    num_workers=8,
    pin_memory=False,
)

for inputs, targets in train_loader:
    inputs = inputs.to("cuda", non_blocking=True)
    targets = targets.to("cuda", non_blocking=True)
    ...
questions.modelAnswer: The specific symptom described, CPU and GPU both under-utilized at once with a visible CPU-ready-to-GPU-visible gap in the profiler, is the signature Lesson-level material identifies for a missing pin_memory combined with non_blocking=True on an unpinned source: non_blocking=True only behaves asynchronously when the source tensor already lives in pinned (page-locked) memory, because the DMA engine needs a fixed physical address to transfer directly; on a pageable (unpinned) source tensor, the driver has to first stage the data through an internal pinned buffer before transferring it, which makes the .to(device, non_blocking=True) call effectively synchronous despite the non_blocking flag, stalling the CPU until that staged copy completes and preventing the intended overlap between the next batch's transfer and the current batch's GPU compute. Here, pin_memory=False on the DataLoader means every batch tensor it produces is ordinary pageable memory, so the non_blocking=True transfers in the training loop never actually get the asynchronous behavior they're asking for, which explains both halves of the symptom: the CPU is blocked waiting on the staged copy (not fully utilized doing useful work, but not idle either) and the GPU is waiting on data that isn't arriving as fast as it could (under-utilized relative to its compute capacity). The fix is simply setting pin_memory=True on the DataLoader, which pre-pins each batch tensor before it reaches the training loop, so the non_blocking=True transfers already in the code finally get genuine asynchronous DMA behavior and can overlap with ongoing GPU compute as intended; num_workers=8 and batch_size=256 are not obviously implicated by this specific symptom and don't need to change based on the evidence given.
questions.professionalAnswer: This exact combination — CPU and GPU both under-utilized at once, plus a visible gap between batch-ready-on-CPU and batch-visible-to-GPU — points pretty specifically at pin_memory being off. non_blocking=True only actually behaves asynchronously if the source tensor is already pinned; on ordinary pageable memory, the driver still has to stage the copy through an internal pinned buffer first, so despite the non_blocking=True in the code, the transfer is effectively synchronous and the CPU just sits there waiting for that staged copy to finish. That's exactly why you'd see both CPU and GPU underutilized together — the CPU's stuck waiting on the staging copy, and the GPU's stuck waiting on data that isn't showing up fast enough, and neither one is actually doing useful work during that gap. The fix is just flipping pin_memory=True on the DataLoader — that pre-pins each batch before it ever reaches the training loop, so non_blocking=True finally does what it's asking for and the next batch's transfer can genuinely overlap with the current batch's GPU compute. I wouldn't touch num_workers or batch_size based on this evidence — the symptom described points specifically at the pinning/transfer path, not at how fast workers are producing batches.
commonMistakes: Assuming non_blocking=True alone guarantees asynchronous transfer regardless of whether the source is pinned
Increasing num_workers as a first fix when the symptom points specifically at the pinning/transfer path, not worker throughput
Not recognizing the specific signature of CPU and GPU both under-utilized at once as pointing at a staging-copy stall
Fixing pin_memory but forgetting it requires both the DataLoader setting and non_blocking=True on the .to() call to actually pay off
Treating this the same as a pure CPU-bound preprocessing bottleneck, which would show a different symptom (CPU pegged near 100%)
keyPoints: non_blocking=True only behaves asynchronously when the source tensor is already pinned memory
pin_memory=False means every batch is pageable, so the transfer silently becomes synchronous despite non_blocking=True
This explains the specific CPU-and-GPU-both-underutilized symptom and the profiler gap
The fix is setting pin_memory=True on the DataLoader
num_workers and batch_size are not implicated by this specific symptom

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies missing pin_memory as the root cause
Correctly explains why non_blocking=True silently becomes synchronous without it
Correctly connects this to the specific observed symptom
Proposes the correct, minimal fix without unnecessary changes

questions.title: Design a Profiling Triage Workflow for an Unexplained Slowdown
questions.prompt: A training job that was previously achieving a known-good step time is now taking roughly 1.8x as long per step, with no code or configuration changes that the team is aware of. Walk through, in order, the specific triage steps you'd actually run to find the cause, and explain why you'd run them in that order rather than jumping straight to the most powerful profiling tool available.
questions.modelAnswer: The right approach is cheapest-and-broadest first, escalating to more expensive, more detailed tools only once the cheap checks have ruled out the common, simple explanations, because jumping straight to the most powerful tool (Nsight Compute's full hardware-counter instrumentation on an arbitrary kernel) is expensive in both engineer time and run time and tells you nothing about which kernel to even look at if you haven't first narrowed down where the problem lives. First, run nvidia-smi dmon across all GPUs for a minute during a slow period to check for an asymmetric utilization pattern (one or more straggler GPUs, or a device-wide drop versus a localized one), which costs nothing and immediately rules in or out a hardware/straggler explanation. Second, check whether the data pipeline is CPU-bound by timing the gap between batches becoming available and the GPU actually consuming them (or simply checking CPU utilization alongside GPU utilization), since a starved GPU waiting on data looks like a slowdown but has nothing to do with the GPU's own kernels. Third, check NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs (for a distributed job) to confirm the all-reduce or other collectives are still using the expected fast transport (NVLink/InfiniBand) rather than having silently fallen back to a slower path, since a transport regression (a bad cable, a misconfigured route, a driver update changing topology detection) is a surprisingly common and otherwise invisible cause of exactly this kind of unexplained, uniform slowdown. Only once all three of those checks are clean, meaning the problem isn't a straggler, isn't the data pipeline, and isn't a communication transport regression, does it make sense to reach for Nsight Systems to get a system-wide timeline and identify which specific kernel or gap is actually consuming the extra time, and only after that narrows it down to a specific kernel does running Nsight Compute's full, expensive instrumentation on that one kernel become worthwhile, rather than running it blindly across the whole model.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always go cheapest-and-broadest first, because the expensive tools are expensive in both run time and the time it takes to actually read their output, and they don't tell you where to look if you haven't already narrowed things down. Step one, costs nothing: nvidia-smi dmon across every GPU for a minute during a slow stretch — that immediately tells me whether this is a straggler problem (one GPU behaving differently from the rest) or a uniform, device-wide slowdown. Step two: check whether the data pipeline's keeping up — is the GPU actually waiting on batches, which looks exactly like a slowdown but has nothing to do with GPU kernels at all. Step three, specific to a distributed job: turn on NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and confirm the collectives are still using the fast transport they were using before — a silently degraded link or a driver update that changed topology detection and fell back to a slower path is a genuinely common cause of 'nothing changed in the code but it got slower,' and it's otherwise completely invisible unless you check it directly. Only once I've ruled all three of those out do I reach for Nsight Systems to get the full timeline and find the specific gap or kernel eating the extra time, and only once that's narrowed to one or two specific kernels does running Nsight Compute's full instrumentation on just those make sense — running it broadly, upfront, without that narrowing is mostly wasted time.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to Nsight Compute's full instrumentation before narrowing down which kernel to even target
Skipping the cheap nvidia-smi dmon check and missing an obvious straggler GPU
Not checking the data pipeline as a possible cause before assuming the slowdown is in GPU kernel execution
Forgetting NCCL transport regression as a cause for a distributed job's 'nothing changed but it's slower' symptom
Running an expensive profiling tool across the whole model instead of narrowing to specific kernels first
keyPoints: Triage proceeds cheapest-and-broadest first, escalating only once simpler checks are clean
nvidia-smi dmon rules a straggler GPU in or out at essentially no cost
Checking the data pipeline rules out a CPU-bound starvation explanation
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO rules out a silent transport regression for distributed jobs
Nsight Systems narrows to specific kernels; Nsight Compute's expensive instrumentation is reserved for those narrowed targets

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes the correct cheapest-first ordering of diagnostic steps
Correctly justifies why each step is checked before the next, more expensive one
Includes the NCCL transport-regression check as a specific, non-obvious step
Correctly places Nsight Systems/Compute as the final, narrowed escalation

questions.title: Write a Progressive-Delivery Rollout Config for a Retrained Model
questions.prompt: Write a canary rollout configuration (as a conceptual YAML sketch for a service mesh or ingress controller) that progressively shifts live traffic from a current production model (champion) to a newly retrained candidate, with an automatic rollback condition. Explain each stage's purpose.
questions.code:
# starting point: 100% of traffic goes to `model-champion`
# candidate `model-challenger` is deployed but receiving 0% of live traffic
questions.modelAnswer: A sound canary rollout defines several progressively larger traffic splits, each held for a soak period long enough to collect a statistically meaningful read on the metrics that matter, with an automatic rollback trigger watching those metrics throughout rather than only at the end. A reasonable structure: stage 1 routes 1% of traffic to model-challenger, held for roughly 30-60 minutes, specifically to catch any gross failure (crashes, obviously wrong outputs, latency blowups) at minimal blast radius before committing more traffic; stage 2 increases to 10%, held for several hours to get a meaningful sample size on business-relevant metrics (not just error rate, but the quality signal the retraining was meant to improve, such as click-through or approval-rate parity); stage 3 increases to 50%, held for at least a full day to capture any day-of-week or traffic-pattern effects a shorter window would miss; and stage 4 completes the cutover to 100% once all prior stages have passed their quality gates. Throughout every stage, an automatic rollback condition should continuously evaluate a small set of hard-gate metrics, for example error rate exceeding the champion's baseline by more than a fixed margin, p99 latency exceeding an SLO threshold, or a business metric dropping below a defined floor, and should revert the traffic split back to 0% on model-challenger immediately if any hard gate trips, rather than waiting for the stage's planned soak period to end, since a canary's entire value is in limiting exposure to a bad model, which requires the rollback to be as fast as the detection.
questions.professionalAnswer: The shape I'd use is a handful of stages, each bigger than the last, each held long enough to actually mean something statistically, with a rollback that can fire at any point, not just at the end of a stage. Something like: 1% for 30-60 minutes just to catch anything grossly broken before it touches real volume; 10% for a few hours once that's clean, long enough to get a real read on the business metric the retraining was actually supposed to move, not just error rate; 50% for a full day to catch any day-of-week effect; then full cutover. The piece I'd be most careful about is the rollback trigger — it needs to be watching continuously throughout every stage, not just checked at the end of a soak window, and it needs hard, pre-agreed thresholds — error rate blowing past the champion's baseline by some margin, p99 latency breaching the SLO, or the business metric dropping below a floor — any one of those should immediately flip traffic back to 0% on the challenger, because the entire point of doing this progressively is limiting how much exposure a genuinely bad model gets, and that only works if detection and rollback are both fast.
questions.example:
# Stage 1: 1% to model-challenger for 30-60 min, hard gate on error_rate and p99_latency
# Stage 2: 10% for several hours, adds business_metric floor check
# Stage 3: 50% for 24h
# Stage 4: 100% cutover
# Rollback: any hard gate breach at any stage -> immediate revert to 0% on model-challenger
commonMistakes: Jumping too aggressively between stages (e.g. 1% straight to 50%) without a meaningful intermediate soak
Checking rollback conditions only at the end of a stage's soak period instead of continuously
Gating only on infrastructure metrics (error rate, latency) without a business-quality metric floor
Not holding later stages long enough to capture day-of-week or traffic-pattern effects
Treating the rollback as a manual, human-triggered action rather than an automatic, fast-firing one
keyPoints: Progressively larger traffic stages, each held for a soak period sized to get a meaningful statistical read
Early stages (1%) catch gross failures at minimal blast radius
Later stages (50%+) need to run long enough to capture day-of-week effects
Rollback conditions should evaluate continuously, not only at stage boundaries
Hard gates should include both infrastructure metrics and the actual business-quality metric being improved

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a reasonable progressive multi-stage traffic-shift structure
Correctly sizes soak periods to get a meaningful read at each stage
Defines a concrete, continuously-evaluated automatic rollback condition
Includes both infrastructure and business-quality metrics in the gate

questions.title: A GPU OOM Appears Mid-Run After an Unrelated Code Change
questions.prompt: A 70B-parameter FSDP training job has run stably for weeks. After a teammate merges a change that only adds a new data augmentation step to the preprocessing pipeline (no changes to the model, optimizer, or FSDP configuration), the job starts OOM-ing roughly 40 minutes into every run, always at a different step. Walk through how you'd diagnose this, given that the change appears unrelated to GPU memory.
questions.modelAnswer: The fact that the failure happens at a different step each time, rather than at a fixed step, is an important clue: a deterministic, fixed-step OOM usually points at a specific input (a pathologically long sequence, a batch with an unusual shape) always appearing at the same point in a fixed data order, whereas a variable-step OOM suggests either a slow, cumulative memory leak that eventually crosses the OOM threshold after enough steps, or a data-dependent spike that happens to occur at different points because the new augmentation step introduces some randomness or variable-sized output that occasionally produces an unusually large tensor. Given the change is 'just' a new data augmentation step, the first hypothesis to check is whether that augmentation can produce variable-sized outputs that weren't possible before, for example a crop/resize/pad step with a bug that occasionally produces a larger-than-intended tensor, since a single oversized batch, even once in thousands of steps, can be enough to push peak memory over the edge in a job that was already running close to its memory ceiling; this is checked by logging the shape of every batch entering the model for a period and looking for outliers, or more surgically, by wrapping a few hundred steps in torch.cuda.memory_allocated() logging to see if there's a spike correlated with a specific batch's shape. The second hypothesis is a genuine memory leak introduced by the augmentation code itself, for example if it accidentally keeps a reference to a tensor alive across iterations (a classic pattern is appending a result to a Python list for logging/debugging purposes without detaching it, keeping its entire autograd graph alive), which would explain a slow, cumulative rise in memory until OOM at a step count that varies slightly run to run depending on exact timing and allocator behavior; this is checked by watching torch.cuda.memory_allocated() (not just memory_reserved()) over the course of a run and confirming whether its baseline between steps is flat or slowly climbing. Since the job was stable for weeks before this specific change and nothing else changed, the augmentation code is the correct place to focus the investigation, and the fix is either bounding/validating its output shape or ensuring it doesn't retain any tensor references across the loop, rather than assuming the FSDP configuration or model code regressed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The variable step-at-failure detail is the thing I'd lean on hardest. If it OOM'd at the exact same step every single run, I'd suspect one specific pathological input sitting at a fixed position in the data order. Since it's different every time, I'm thinking either a slow leak that accumulates until it crosses the ceiling at a slightly different point run to run, or the new augmentation occasionally produces an oversized output due to some randomness in it, and which batch happens to trigger that is itself somewhat random. Given the only actual change here is the new augmentation step, that's where I'd focus, not the model or FSDP config that didn't change and ran stably for weeks. First thing I'd do is log the shape of every batch coming out of that augmentation for a few hundred steps and look for an outlier — a crop or resize bug that occasionally emits something larger than intended is a really common, boring cause, and even one oversized batch can push a job that's already near its memory ceiling over the edge. Second thing, in parallel: watch torch.cuda.memory_allocated() (the actual allocated figure, not just reserved) across a run's steps and see if the baseline between steps is flat or slowly creeping up — if it's creeping, that points at a leak, probably something in the new augmentation code holding onto a tensor reference it shouldn't, a classic pattern being appending something to a list for logging without detaching it first and keeping its whole autograd graph pinned in memory.
questions.example: A new RandomResizedCrop-style augmentation has a bug where, for a small fraction of inputs with an unusual aspect ratio, it occasionally produces an output 3x the intended size; this surfaces as an OOM only when that rare input shape happens to land in the current batch, explaining why the failing step varies run to run.
commonMistakes: Assuming the FSDP or model configuration regressed despite being unchanged, ignoring the one actual change that was made
Treating a variable failing step the same as a deterministic, fixed-step failure and misdiagnosing accordingly
Checking memory_reserved() instead of memory_allocated() when looking for a genuine leak versus allocator caching behavior
Not logging batch shapes to check for an outlier produced by the new augmentation
Reverting the augmentation change without first confirming which of the two hypotheses (oversized output vs. leak) actually explains the failure
keyPoints: A variable failing step points at either a cumulative leak or a data-dependent spike, not a fixed pathological input
The newly added augmentation step is the correct focus, since it's the one actual change before stable weeks
Logging batch shapes can surface an occasional oversized output from a buggy augmentation
Watching memory_allocated() over time distinguishes a genuine leak from normal allocator behavior
A common leak pattern is retaining an undetached tensor reference (e.g. in a logging list) across iterations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about the significance of the variable (not fixed) failing step
Correctly focuses the investigation on the one actual change made
Proposes concrete, correct diagnostic steps for both the oversized-output and leak hypotheses
Distinguishes memory_allocated from memory_reserved appropriately

questions.title: A DDP Job Regresses in Throughput With No Code Changes
questions.prompt: A 4-GPU DDP training job on a single node has been running at a known-good throughput for months. This morning, with no code or config changes, the same job takes twice as long per step. The team is convinced something must have changed. Walk through your diagnostic approach and name the most likely class of cause given that nothing in the training code changed.
questions.modelAnswer: When the training code and configuration are genuinely unchanged but throughput regresses, the most likely class of cause is something that changed in the environment underneath the code: a driver or CUDA version update pushed by an automated maintenance window, a degraded or reconfigured NVLink/PCIe topology (if the node was ever rebooted or had hardware serviced), a noisy neighbor on a shared node competing for PCIe or memory bandwidth, or a change in which physical GPUs the job landed on if the cluster scheduler isn't pinning GPU affinity consistently. The diagnostic approach should follow the same cheapest-first order regardless of the specific hypothesis: first, nvidia-smi dmon across all 4 GPUs to check for a straggler (one GPU behaving differently from the other three, which would point at a specific hardware or placement issue rather than a uniform regression); second, nvidia-smi topo -m to confirm the NVLink/PCIe topology between the 4 GPUs still matches what it was before, since a changed topology (for example, after a reboot, if the GPUs ended up reassigned to different PCIe slots with a different connection type) would directly explain a uniform slowdown in DDP's gradient all-reduce without any code change; third, checking NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs to confirm NCCL is still selecting the same transport it used to (NVLink between GPUs on this node) rather than having fallen back to a slower path, which can happen silently after a driver update changes how NCCL detects the topology. Given that nothing in the code changed and the regression is uniform across the job (not isolated to one GPU, per the hypothesis that should be checked first), the most likely single class of cause is an environment-level change: a driver/CUDA update altering NCCL's topology detection or transport selection is specifically worth checking first, since it's a common, often-overlooked cause of 'nothing changed but it got slower' that wouldn't show up in any code diff the team would think to look at.
questions.professionalAnswer: 'Nothing changed' almost always means 'nothing changed in the code,' and the environment underneath the code is exactly where I'd look first — a driver update from an automated maintenance window, a node reboot that changed which PCIe slots the GPUs landed in, a noisy neighbor process competing for the same node's PCIe bandwidth, anything like that can regress throughput with zero code diff to point at. I'd start with the same cheap checks regardless of which specific cause turns out to be right: nvidia-smi dmon across all 4 GPUs first, to see if this is a straggler-GPU problem (one GPU behaving differently) or a genuinely uniform slowdown across all four. If it's uniform, nvidia-smi topo -m next, to confirm the NVLink/PCIe topology between the GPUs is actually what it was before — a reboot landing GPUs in different slots with a worse interconnect path is a real, common, invisible-to-code-review cause. And I'd turn on NCCL_DEBUG=INFO to confirm NCCL's still picking NVLink for the all-reduce rather than having silently fallen back to something slower, which does happen after driver updates change how topology gets detected. My actual bet, given it's uniform and nothing in the code changed, is a driver or topology change under the hood — that's the class of cause I'd chase first before assuming anything subtler is going on.
questions.example: A routine OS patch window updated the NVIDIA driver overnight; the new driver version changed how NCCL probes NVLink topology on this motherboard, and NCCL silently fell back to a PCIe-only path for the all-reduce instead of NVLink, roughly doubling gradient-sync time with zero change to the training code.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'no code changes' means the environment is also unchanged
Jumping to a data-pipeline explanation before checking GPU utilization symmetry across the 4 GPUs
Not checking nvidia-smi topo -m to confirm the interconnect topology actually matches what it was before
Skipping NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, missing a silent transport fallback after a driver update
Not considering a noisy-neighbor or automated maintenance-window explanation for a single-node environment change
keyPoints: An unchanged codebase with a regressed throughput points at an environment-level change, not a logic bug
Driver/CUDA updates, topology changes from a reboot, and noisy neighbors are the likely candidate causes
Checking for a straggler GPU first distinguishes a uniform regression from a localized one
nvidia-smi topo -m and NCCL_DEBUG=INFO specifically surface topology and transport-selection regressions
This class of cause is easy to miss because it never shows up in a code diff

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies environment-level change as the most likely cause class
Proposes a sensible, correctly ordered diagnostic sequence
Specifically checks topology and NCCL transport selection
Gives a concrete, plausible root-cause scenario

questions.title: A Serving Fleet's Latency Spikes Under a Sudden Traffic Shift
questions.prompt: A vLLM-based serving fleet has met its p99 TTFT SLO reliably for months. After a product launch shifts traffic toward a feature that sends much longer prompts (average prompt length roughly tripled), p99 TTFT blows past the SLO even though total request volume (requests/sec) barely changed. Walk through the diagnosis and explain why request volume alone was the wrong thing to watch.
questions.modelAnswer: Requests per second measures how often requests arrive, but it says nothing about how much work each request actually requires; prefill is compute-bound and its cost scales with prompt length, so tripling average prompt length roughly triples the compute work the prefill phase has to do per request even if the number of requests per second is unchanged, which means the fleet's actual compute load went up substantially even though the metric the team was watching (RPS) looked flat. This explains the TTFT regression directly: TTFT is dominated by time spent in prefill plus any queuing delay before a request is admitted into a batch, and if each request's prefill now takes roughly three times as long, either the GPU spends three times as long per request in the compute-bound prefill phase (directly inflating TTFT for every request), or, if the fleet's batching/concurrency settings assumed the old, shorter prompt length when computing how many requests to admit concurrently, the KV cache and compute budget per batch now gets consumed by fewer, longer requests, pushing more incoming requests into a queue and inflating the tail of the queuing-delay distribution specifically, which is exactly the kind of nonlinear, near-saturation growth that explains why p99 degraded far more than you'd expect from an apparently modest 3x change, even though p50 may have moved less dramatically. The fix requires reconsidering capacity in terms of actual compute/token load, not request count: recompute how many concurrent long-prompt requests the fleet's KV cache and compute budget can actually sustain within the TTFT SLO (potentially requiring more replicas, or chunked prefill to prevent a single long prompt's prefill from stalling other in-flight requests' decode steps), rather than assuming the fleet sized for the old traffic pattern automatically handles a traffic mix shift that leaves RPS unchanged but substantially increases per-request work.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mistake the team made, understandably, is watching RPS as a proxy for load, when RPS only tells you how often requests show up, not how much work each one actually costs. Prefill is compute-bound and scales with prompt length, so tripling average prompt length roughly triples the compute cost per request even with the exact same RPS — the fleet's actual load went up a lot, the metric everyone was watching just didn't show it. That explains the TTFT blowup directly: either each request's own prefill phase is just taking three times as long now, which inflates TTFT on its own, or the fleet's batching assumptions, tuned for the old, shorter prompts, mean the GPU's compute and KV-cache budget gets eaten up by fewer, longer requests per batch than before, so more requests end up waiting in queue — and queuing delay is exactly the kind of thing that blows out the p99 tail disproportionately once you're near saturation, even if the median barely moves. The fix isn't 'add capacity based on RPS,' it's recomputing capacity based on actual compute load — how many concurrent long-prompt requests can this fleet's compute and KV cache budget actually sustain within the TTFT SLO — and that probably means more replicas, and possibly chunked prefill so one long prompt's prefill doesn't stall decode steps for requests already in flight.
questions.example: Average prompt length goes from 500 to 1,500 tokens with RPS unchanged; prefill compute per request roughly triples, and because the fleet's concurrency limits were tuned assuming 500-token prompts, incoming requests now queue behind longer-running prefills, pushing p99 TTFT well past SLO while p50 degrades more modestly.
commonMistakes: Treating RPS as a sufficient proxy for actual GPU load without accounting for per-request work
Not connecting prompt length specifically to prefill's compute-bound cost
Assuming p50 and p99 would degrade proportionally, missing why tail latency is disproportionately affected near saturation
Fixing this by scaling replica count based on RPS rather than actual compute/token load
Not considering chunked prefill as a mitigation for long prompts stalling other in-flight requests
keyPoints: RPS measures request frequency, not per-request compute cost
Prefill is compute-bound and scales with prompt length, so longer prompts substantially increase load even at flat RPS
This explains the TTFT regression via either direct per-request prefill cost or increased queuing delay
Tail latency (p99) degrades disproportionately near saturation compared to p50
Capacity planning should be based on compute/token load, not request count alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why RPS was the wrong signal to watch
Correctly connects prompt length to prefill's compute-bound cost
Correctly explains the disproportionate tail-latency effect near saturation
Proposes a concrete, correct remediation approach

questions.title: A Kubernetes GPU Job Repeatedly Lands Pending Despite Idle Capacity
questions.prompt: A team's PyTorchJob requesting 8 nodes with 8 GPUs each repeatedly sits with 2 of its 8 worker pods Pending, even though `kubectl describe node` on several nodes shows 8 idle A100s each. The job previously ran successfully at this exact size last week. Walk through the diagnosis.
questions.modelAnswer: Since the exact same job size ran successfully last week, the first thing to check is what's different about the cluster's current state rather than the job's own configuration, which likely hasn't changed. Relevant candidates: whether the specific GPU type requested (if the PodGroup or node affinity constrains to a particular GPU model or MIG profile) is actually available in sufficient quantity right now, since 'idle A100s' visible via kubectl describe node doesn't guarantee they match whatever node selector or resource request the job specifies, for example if some nodes are configured with MIG partitioning and the job is requesting whole, non-partitioned GPUs that those specific MIG-partitioned nodes can no longer offer; whether a competing job or queue is holding a reservation (common with Volcano or similar gang-scheduling queues, where a queue's capability or weight could be currently capping how much of the cluster this job's queue can claim even if raw node capacity is technically idle); and whether the 2 Pending pods specifically are being blocked by a node affinity, taint/toleration, or topology-spread constraint that happens to route them toward a subset of nodes that, this week, don't have the needed capacity (for example, if 2 of the previously-available nodes were cordoned for maintenance and the constraint doesn't let the scheduler use other otherwise-idle nodes). The diagnostic sequence should be: run kubectl describe pod on one of the 2 Pending pods to read its exact FailedScheduling reason, which will usually name the specific constraint (insufficient GPU of the right type, taint mismatch, affinity mismatch) rather than a generic 'insufficient resources' message; cross-reference that against kubectl get nodes -o wide plus kubectl describe node on the specific nodes the scheduler considered, checking labels, taints, and whether MIG partitioning changed; and check the Volcano queue (or equivalent) status for this job's queue to confirm its capability/weight configuration still matches what it was last week, since queue configuration (not raw cluster capacity) is a common source of this exact symptom when a job's size is genuinely unchanged.
questions.professionalAnswer: The job being identical to a run that worked last week is the key detail — it tells me to look at what's different about the cluster right now, not at the job's own config. kubectl describe pod on one of the Pending pods is always my first move, because it'll usually name the actual constraint in the FailedScheduling reason rather than me having to guess — insufficient GPUs of a specific type, a taint mismatch, an affinity constraint pointing at nodes that don't currently qualify. My short list of suspects: maybe some nodes got reconfigured with MIG partitioning since last week, so 'idle A100s' on kubectl describe node doesn't mean they're idle whole-GPU A100s the way this job's requesting; maybe a couple of the nodes this job's affinity would normally land on got cordoned for maintenance, and the constraint doesn't let the scheduler fall back to other idle nodes; or, if this cluster uses Volcano or similar queueing, maybe the job's queue capability or weight got adjusted and it's now capped below what it needs, even though total cluster capacity is fine. I'd check the pod's actual scheduling failure reason first, then cross-reference node labels/taints and whether anything about MIG configuration changed, then check the queue status specifically if that's in play — because 'the job is unchanged but the cluster isn't' is exactly the kind of thing kubectl describe node's raw idle-GPU count won't show you directly.
