questions.example: Two of the cluster's nodes were reconfigured last week to run MIG-partitioned A100 instances for a different team's workload; kubectl describe node still shows '8 GPUs' listed per node, but the allocatable resource is now nvidia.com/mig-1g.5gb rather than whole nvidia.com/gpu units, which the job's request doesn't match, leaving its pods Pending even though raw GPU hardware looks idle.
commonMistakes: Assuming the job's own configuration must have regressed when it was previously identical and working
Treating 'idle GPUs shown on the node' as equivalent to 'GPUs matching this job's exact resource request'
Not running kubectl describe pod first to read the specific FailedScheduling reason before guessing
Overlooking queue-level (Volcano or equivalent) capability/weight changes as a cause distinct from raw node capacity
Not checking whether node taints, cordons, or MIG reconfiguration changed since the last successful run
keyPoints: An unchanged job with a new failure points at what changed in the cluster environment
'Idle GPUs' on a node doesn't guarantee they match the job's exact resource type (e.g. MIG vs. whole GPU)
kubectl describe pod's FailedScheduling reason should be read first, before guessing at causes
Queue-level capability/weight configuration can block a job even with idle raw cluster capacity
Taints, cordons, and MIG reconfiguration are concrete, checkable candidates for what changed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that an unchanged job points at a changed cluster environment
Correctly distinguishes raw idle GPU capacity from capacity matching the exact request
Proposes checking the pod's specific FailedScheduling reason first
Names concrete, plausible candidate causes (MIG, taints, queue config)

questions.title: An NCCL Watchdog Timeout Hangs a Multi-Node Job
questions.prompt: A 128-GPU training job hangs mid-step and, after several minutes, NCCL's watchdog fires a timeout error on most ranks, naming an all-reduce call. The job had run cleanly for 6 hours before this happened. Walk through how you'd distinguish between the main plausible causes (a single straggler/dead GPU, a network partition, and a genuine deadlock in the collective call pattern itself).
questions.modelAnswer: NCCL's watchdog exists specifically to convert a hang (which would otherwise block forever with no signal) into an explicit, visible timeout error, and the fact that it fired on most ranks naming the same all-reduce call is itself informative: it means most ranks reached that collective and are waiting on it, which already rules out the simplest version of 'the collective call pattern itself is wrong' (a genuine code-level deadlock, such as two ranks calling different collectives in a different order, would typically manifest as a mismatch error or a hang with no consistent pattern across ranks, not a clean timeout on the same named call everywhere). To distinguish a dead/straggler GPU from a network partition: check whether the ranks that did NOT report the timeout (if any) correspond to a specific node or a specific small set of GPUs, since a dead or badly straggling GPU would manifest as that specific rank's process having already crashed, hung, or logged an Xid error in dmesg/nvidia-smi before the watchdog even fired elsewhere, which is checkable by looking at that rank's own process state and the node's GPU health (nvidia-smi, Xid error logs) directly, independent of NCCL's own logs. A network partition, by contrast, would typically show no GPU-level hardware signal on any node, but would show NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs (if enabled ahead of time, or re-enabled for the retry) indicating a specific pair or subset of ranks failing to complete their send/receive within the collective, often correlated with switch or NIC-level alerts from the network monitoring stack rather than any GPU-level symptom. Given the job ran cleanly for 6 hours before this, a transient hardware fault (a GPU falling off the bus, an Xid error, a NIC flapping) is statistically the most common real-world cause at this scale, consistent with the earlier reasoning about compounding per-GPU and per-NIC failure probabilities across 128 GPUs over a multi-hour window, so checking node-level hardware signals (dmesg, Xid logs, ibstat/perfquery on the InfiniBand ports) for every node involved should be the first concrete step, ahead of assuming a code-level deadlock, since nothing about the job's collective call pattern changed between the clean 6 hours and the hang.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fact that the timeout fired on most ranks, all naming the same all-reduce call, already tells me something — a genuine code-level deadlock, like two ranks calling collectives in a mismatched order, usually looks messier than that, often a collective-mismatch error or an inconsistent hang pattern, not a clean, uniform timeout on the same call everywhere. Since nothing about the collective call pattern changed in the 6 hours the job ran cleanly before this, I'd put a code-level deadlock lower on my list and focus on hardware or network first. To tell a dead/straggler GPU from a network partition, I'd check whether there's a specific rank or node that behaves differently from the rest — a dead GPU usually leaves its own signal behind independent of NCCL: an Xid error in dmesg, nvidia-smi reporting the GPU in a bad state, or that specific process having already crashed before the watchdog even fired for everyone else. A network partition instead tends to show no GPU-level symptom anywhere, but does show up in NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs as a specific pair or subset of ranks failing to complete their part of the collective, often alongside something from the network monitoring side — a flapping NIC, a switch alert. Given six clean hours beforehand and 128 GPUs running that whole time, my actual bet, statistically, is a transient hardware fault somewhere — a GPU falling off the bus or a flaky NIC — so my first concrete step is checking dmesg and Xid logs across every node involved, and the InfiniBand port counters, before I'd spend time looking at the collective call pattern in the code, which didn't change.
questions.example: dmesg on node 47 shows an Xid 79 error (GPU has fallen off the bus) logged roughly 90 seconds before the NCCL watchdog timeout fired cluster-wide; the other 127 ranks were all correctly waiting on rank 376 (on node 47) to reach the all-reduce, which it never did because its GPU had already failed.
commonMistakes: Jumping to a code-level deadlock explanation despite the job having run cleanly for 6 hours with no code changes
Not recognizing that a uniform timeout naming the same collective across most ranks is itself informative evidence
Treating NCCL's own logs as sufficient without checking node-level hardware signals (dmesg, Xid, nvidia-smi) directly
Not distinguishing the GPU-hardware-fault signature (independent of NCCL) from the network-partition signature (visible mainly through NCCL/network logs)
Ignoring the statistical argument that a single transient hardware fault is the most common cause at this scale over a multi-hour window
keyPoints: A uniform timeout on the same named collective across most ranks argues against a messy, code-level deadlock
A dead/straggler GPU leaves an independent hardware signal (Xid, dmesg, nvidia-smi state) checkable without NCCL logs
A network partition tends to show no GPU-level signal but shows up in NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and network monitoring
6 clean hours beforehand with no code change argues against a collective-call-pattern bug
At 128-GPU scale over multiple hours, a transient hardware fault is statistically the most likely real-world cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about what the uniform timeout pattern implies
Correctly distinguishes the hardware-fault signature from the network-partition signature
Correctly deprioritizes a code-level deadlock given the evidence
Proposes concrete, correctly ordered diagnostic steps

questions.title: A Loss Curve Spikes to NaN at a Specific Step Every Time
questions.prompt: A large model's training loss spikes to NaN at exactly step 14,200, reproducibly across multiple restarts from the same checkpoint with the same data order. The team suspects the learning rate schedule, but the spike happens at the same step regardless of what the base learning rate is set to (tested at both the original value and half of it). Walk through what this rules in and out, and what you'd check next.
questions.modelAnswer: The fact that the NaN occurs at exactly the same step regardless of learning rate, and reproducibly across restarts from the same checkpoint with the same data order, strongly argues against a generic 'learning rate too high' explanation, because an LR-driven divergence would typically be sensitive to the actual LR value (a halved LR would at minimum shift when or whether the divergence occurs, even if it didn't eliminate it entirely); instead, this pattern points at something deterministic in the data or the model's numerical state that is specific to whatever is happening at that exact step, independent of the optimizer's step size. The leading hypothesis given reproducibility tied to data order is a specific, pathological batch at step 14,200: a batch containing an outlier input (an unusually long sequence, a corrupted or mislabeled example, an input containing a value like infinity or an extreme outlier after some data-cleaning edge case) that produces an extreme activation or loss value regardless of the learning rate, since the LR scales the update step but doesn't change whether the forward pass itself produces an extreme value. A second, related hypothesis is a numerical edge case in the model's own forward computation that's deterministic given the model's exact parameter state at that step, for example an attention computation dividing by a near-zero value, or an exponential/log operation receiving an input that happens to be in a problematic numerical range at that specific point in training, which again wouldn't be LR-sensitive since it's a property of the forward computation, not the update step. The concrete next steps are: log and inspect the exact batch(es) processed in the steps immediately before and at 14,200 for any input-level outlier (sequence length, extreme numeric values, anomalous labels); add activation and gradient-norm logging per-layer in the steps leading up to 14,200 to see whether a specific layer's activations or gradients were already growing abnormally large before the NaN, which would point at a specific operation rather than the data itself; and check whether AMP/GradScaler was in play, since even with GradScaler, a single extreme value can occasionally produce an inf that GradScaler's own skip-step logic should catch and recover from, so a true NaN surfacing in the loss (rather than being caught and skipped) suggests the extreme value occurred somewhere GradScaler's inf-checking doesn't cover, such as inside the forward pass's loss computation itself rather than in the gradients.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that kills the 'learning rate is too high' theory pretty cleanly is that halving the LR didn't change when it happens — if this were a genuine LR-driven divergence, I'd expect the specific step (or at least whether it diverges at all) to be sensitive to the actual LR value, and it isn't. Since it's deterministic to the exact same step across restarts with the same data order, that points at something about what's happening at that specific step in the data or the model's numerical state, not the optimizer's step size. My leading theory is a specific bad batch at step 14,200 — an outlier input, maybe an unusually long sequence or a corrupted example that produces an extreme value in the forward pass regardless of how big the subsequent update step is, because the learning rate scales the update, it doesn't change whether the forward pass itself blows up. I'd log and actually look at the batch going into step 14,200 for anything that stands out — sequence length, weird numeric values, a mislabeled example. In parallel I'd add per-layer activation and gradient-norm logging for the steps leading up to it, to see whether some specific layer's values were already climbing abnormally before the NaN actually showed up, which would point me at a specific operation rather than the input data. And I'd check whether GradScaler is in the mix — if it is, a true NaN surfacing in the loss rather than being caught by GradScaler's own skip-step logic tells me the extreme value probably occurred inside the forward pass's loss computation itself, somewhere GradScaler's inf-checking on gradients doesn't actually cover.
questions.example: Step 14,200's batch happens to contain a sequence with a data-cleaning bug that left one token's embedding index set to an out-of-vocabulary value mapping to an uninitialized or garbage embedding row; the forward pass through that token produces an extreme activation that propagates to a NaN loss regardless of the learning rate, since it's a forward-pass numerical issue, not an update-step-size issue.
commonMistakes: Continuing to tune the learning rate after evidence (LR-insensitivity) already argues against an LR-driven cause
Not recognizing that reproducibility at the exact same step with the same data order is a strong clue pointing at the data or a deterministic numerical edge case
Assuming GradScaler would always catch an extreme value before it reaches the loss, when the issue could occur in the forward pass itself
Not logging per-layer activation/gradient norms before the failing step to localize which operation is involved
Skipping direct inspection of the actual batch content at the failing step
keyPoints: LR-insensitivity of the failing step argues strongly against a learning-rate-driven divergence
Determinism tied to data order points at a specific pathological batch or a deterministic numerical edge case
The LR scales the update step but doesn't change whether the forward pass itself produces an extreme value
Per-layer activation/gradient-norm logging before the failing step can localize the responsible operation
A true NaN surfacing despite GradScaler suggests the issue occurs somewhere its inf-checking doesn't cover

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that LR-insensitivity argues against an LR-driven cause
Correctly connects data-order determinism to a specific-batch or numerical-edge-case hypothesis
Proposes concrete, correct diagnostic logging (batch inspection, per-layer norms)
Correctly reasons about GradScaler's coverage limits

questions.title: A Model's Quality Degrades Silently With No Errors or Infra Alerts
questions.prompt: A recommendation model's business-metric dashboard (click-through rate) shows a slow, steady decline over three weeks. No error-rate alert, latency alert, or infrastructure dashboard shows anything unusual, and no new model version was deployed during this window. Walk through how you'd investigate a problem that isn't showing up anywhere in standard monitoring.
questions.modelAnswer: The absence of any infrastructure or error-rate signal, combined with no model redeployment, strongly suggests the problem is upstream of the model itself (the input data) or a slow distributional shift in the real world the model wasn't trained to handle, rather than a software bug or a bad deploy, since both of those would typically produce some infrastructure-visible symptom. The systematic triage, in order: first, confirm the serving model version genuinely hasn't changed, not just that no deploy was logged, by checking the actual model artifact hash currently being served against the known-good version, since a silent, unintended redeploy (for example from an autoscaler rolling pods with a stale or mismatched image tag) is a real, if less likely, possibility worth ruling out cheaply before looking elsewhere. Second, check feature freshness: confirm the features feeding this model are being updated on the schedule they're supposed to be, since a silently stale upstream feature (a batch job that started failing partway without alerting, or quietly started succeeding on incomplete data) would degrade the model's effective inputs without producing any infrastructure error, since the pipeline itself may be 'succeeding' from a monitoring perspective while the data it produces becomes progressively staler or less complete. Third, and most likely given a slow three-week decline rather than a sudden drop, check feature distribution for drift: run a population stability index (PSI) or similar distributional comparison between the current window's feature values and the training-time distribution, since a slow upstream shift, such as a change in the user population mix, a new client platform sending subtly different interaction signal shapes, or a seasonal behavior change the training data didn't cover, would produce exactly this symptom, a model whose inputs have quietly drifted out of the distribution it was trained and validated on, degrading prediction quality gradually with no infrastructure signal anywhere, because nothing about serving the model is actually broken, the inputs it's correctly serving on have just changed. The fix, once the specific drifted feature or segment is identified, is typically a feature killswitch or fallback to a safe default for the affected inputs while the root cause (stale upstream data, or a genuine population shift requiring retraining) is addressed, followed by instituting an automated drift check as a standing SLO so the next occurrence surfaces proactively rather than through a slow dashboard decline someone eventually notices.
questions.professionalAnswer: No infra signal and no redeploy is itself a strong clue — it tells me to look upstream of the model, at the data going in, rather than at the model-serving stack, which would usually leave some trace if it were broken. I'd start cheap: actually confirm the model version being served hasn't silently changed — check the artifact hash currently live against the known-good one, not just trust that nobody logged a deploy, because an autoscaler rolling pods onto a stale image is a real, if boring, possibility worth ruling out first. Then I'd check feature freshness — is whatever feeds this model's inputs actually updating on schedule, because a batch job that started quietly failing or started succeeding on incomplete data wouldn't necessarily trip any infra alert, it'd just mean the model's inputs are gradually going stale. But given this is a slow three-week decline, not a cliff, my real bet is feature drift — I'd run a PSI check comparing the current feature distribution against the training-time distribution, because a slow shift in the underlying population — new users, a new client platform sending slightly different signals, a seasonal behavior change — produces exactly this symptom: nothing's broken in any infrastructure sense, the model's correctly serving on inputs that have just quietly moved away from what it was trained on. Once I've found the specific drifted feature or segment, I'd flip a killswitch or fallback for the affected inputs while the real fix — retraining on the new distribution, or fixing stale upstream data — gets sorted, and I'd turn the manual PSI check I just ran by hand into a standing automated drift alert so this surfaces on its own next time instead of someone noticing a slow dashboard decline three weeks in.
questions.example: A mobile app update changed how a client-side feature (session duration) is computed, subtly shifting its distribution; the pipeline reports success on every run since it's syntactically valid data, but the feature's values no longer match what the model was trained to expect, degrading click-through prediction quality gradually with zero infrastructure-visible symptom.
commonMistakes: Assuming the absence of error-rate/latency alerts means nothing is wrong, rather than that the problem is upstream of infrastructure
Not confirming the actually-served model version against its known-good hash before looking elsewhere
Jumping straight to 'retrain the model' without first identifying the specific drifted feature or segment
Not distinguishing a slow, gradual decline (pointing at drift) from a sudden drop (which would point elsewhere)
Treating a pipeline reporting 'success' as proof the data it produced is actually fresh and complete
keyPoints: No infra/error signal plus no redeploy points upstream of the model, at the data or a real-world distribution shift
Confirming the actually-served model version (artifact hash) rules out a silent, unintended redeploy cheaply
Feature freshness checks catch silently stale upstream data that a 'successful' pipeline run can mask
A slow, multi-week decline is the classic signature of gradual feature/population drift, checked via PSI
The fix pairs an immediate killswitch/fallback with a standing automated drift-detection SLO going forward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that the problem is likely upstream of model-serving infrastructure
Proposes a sensible, correctly ordered triage sequence
Correctly identifies feature/distributional drift as the leading hypothesis for a slow decline
Proposes both an immediate mitigation and a lasting, automated fix

questions.title: An Elastic Training Job Burns Through Its Restart Budget
questions.prompt: A training job using torch.distributed.elastic with --nnodes=8:32 and --max-restarts=5, running mostly on spot/preemptible capacity, keeps failing permanently after exactly 5 restart attempts, even though the job has made real forward progress each time before being interrupted. Diagnose why the restart budget is being exhausted and propose concrete fixes.
questions.modelAnswer: max-restarts caps how many times the elastic agent will attempt to re-form the worker group before permanently failing the job, and that counter increments on every re-formation event regardless of how much progress was made in between, which means a job running on spot capacity with a reclamation rate high enough to trigger a Worker disappearing and rejoining more than 5 times total will exhaust the budget purely from the cumulative count of individual preemption events, not from any lack of real progress; the job described is making real forward progress each time but is still being preempted often enough, cumulatively, to hit 5 restarts and fail, which indicates the restart budget itself is undersized for the actual preemption rate of the spot capacity this job is running on, not that something is fundamentally broken in the training logic. The fix has two complementary parts: first, raise --max-restarts to a value that reflects the realistic preemption frequency of the spot pool over the job's expected total runtime, since a budget of 5 is clearly too small if preemptions recur more than 5 times over a multi-day run, which is a straightforward, low-risk configuration change; second, and more structurally, separate restart cost from restart count by ensuring checkpointing happens frequently enough that each individual restart loses only a small, bounded amount of work, since the actual problem worth solving isn't 'the job restarted many times,' it's whether restarting is cheap, and if checkpoint-interval is too coarse, frequent preemptions on spot capacity compound into large amounts of lost progress even before the restart-budget ceiling is reached. A third, complementary mitigation worth considering is keeping a minimum floor of on-demand (non-preemptible) capacity for a subset of the job's nodes, which doesn't eliminate the Worker churn on the remaining spot nodes but reduces the overall preemption frequency the job experiences, directly reducing how often the restart counter increments in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: max-restarts counts every single re-formation event, full stop, regardless of how much real progress happened between them — so if this job's genuinely making progress each time but is on a spot pool getting reclaimed often enough to trigger more than 5 total preemptions over its runtime, it's going to hit that ceiling and fail permanently even though nothing about the training itself is broken. That tells me the actual problem is the restart budget being sized too small for how often this spot pool actually gets reclaimed, not a training-logic bug. The straightforward fix is just raising max-restarts to something that reflects the real preemption rate over the job's expected total runtime — if preemptions happen, say, twice a day and the job runs for a week, 5 was never going to be enough. The more structural fix, though, is making each individual restart cheap rather than just allowing more of them — that means checking the checkpoint interval is tight enough that a preemption only loses a small, bounded amount of progress, because the actual thing that matters isn't the restart count, it's how much work each restart throws away. And I'd look at whether it's worth putting a floor of on-demand, non-preemptible capacity under a subset of the nodes — that doesn't fix the restart budget math directly, but it reduces how often the job gets preempted in the first place, which is the root cause driving the counter up in the first place.
questions.example: A job on a spot pool with an average reclamation interval of roughly 8 hours, running for 4 days, experiences about 12 preemption events total; with max-restarts=5, the job fails permanently after the 5th, even though each restart resumed cleanly from a recent checkpoint and made real progress in between.
commonMistakes: Assuming the job failing after exactly 5 restarts indicates a training-logic bug rather than an undersized restart budget
Raising max-restarts without also checking whether checkpoint frequency bounds the cost of each individual restart
Not considering a mixed on-demand/spot capacity floor as a way to reduce the underlying preemption rate itself
Treating restart count and lost progress as the same problem, when they're separate (frequency vs. cost per event)
Not estimating the realistic preemption frequency of the spot pool before picking a new max-restarts value
keyPoints: max-restarts counts every re-formation event, regardless of progress made between them
A job genuinely progressing can still exhaust the budget if preemptions recur often enough
The straightforward fix is sizing max-restarts to the pool's realistic preemption frequency
The structural fix is tightening checkpoint interval so each restart's cost (lost work) stays small
A partial floor of on-demand capacity reduces the underlying preemption rate itself

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that max-restarts counts events, not lack of progress
Correctly diagnoses the budget as undersized for the actual preemption rate
Proposes raising max-restarts appropriately
Proposes the structural checkpoint-frequency fix and/or on-demand floor mitigation

questions.title: A CPU-Based Autoscaler Fails to Scale a GPU Serving Fleet
questions.prompt: A vLLM serving deployment's Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is configured to scale on CPU utilization, the Kubernetes default. Under a real traffic surge, requests visibly queue and p99 latency blows past SLO, but the HPA never triggers a scale-out, and CPU utilization graphs show the pods sitting around 15% the entire time. Diagnose why, and propose the correct autoscaling signal.
questions.modelAnswer: For a GPU-bound inference workload, the CPU does comparatively little of the actual work: tokenization, request routing, and light orchestration happen on CPU, but the dominant cost, the model's forward pass during prefill and decode, runs entirely on the GPU, so CPU utilization stays low even when the service is fully saturated and actively queuing requests, which is exactly what the 15% CPU reading during a real traffic surge reflects, not a sign that the service has spare capacity. Because the HPA is configured to scale on this metric specifically, it never sees evidence that anything is wrong, since from CPU utilization's perspective, the pods genuinely are idle-looking, and the HPA has no visibility into GPU saturation, KV cache pressure, or request queue depth at all unless explicitly configured to watch those signals instead. The correct autoscaling signal for a GPU-bound serving fleet should be something that actually tracks inference load: queue depth (how many requests are waiting for a batch slot), in-flight request count relative to the fleet's known per-replica capacity, GPU utilization itself (via a custom metrics adapter exposing DCGM or nvidia-smi-derived metrics to the HPA), or a latency-based signal (such as current p95/p99 TTFT measured per replica) are all meaningfully correlated with actual inference saturation in a way CPU utilization is not. In practice, most teams implement this via the Kubernetes custom metrics API or an external metrics adapter (such as Prometheus Adapter) exposing a GPU- or queue-based metric that the HPA can scale on, replacing or supplementing the default CPU-based target entirely; without that change, this fleet will continue to silently fail to scale under every future traffic surge regardless of how badly latency degrades, since CPU utilization simply isn't correlated with the thing that's actually saturating.
questions.professionalAnswer: The CPU metric is just the wrong signal entirely for this kind of workload, and 15% CPU during a real surge isn't evidence of spare capacity, it's evidence that CPU was never doing the expensive work in the first place — tokenization and routing are cheap, the actual cost is the GPU forward pass during prefill and decode, and CPU utilization has no visibility into that at all. So the HPA isn't malfunctioning, it's correctly reading a metric that's just disconnected from what's actually saturating. The fix is switching to a signal that actually tracks inference load — queue depth is probably my first choice, since it directly measures 'how many requests are waiting for a batch slot right now,' but GPU utilization itself (piped through a custom metrics adapter from DCGM or nvidia-smi) or a latency-based signal like current p95 TTFT per replica all work too, and some teams use more than one combined. In Kubernetes terms that means wiring up the custom metrics API, commonly via something like Prometheus Adapter, so the HPA has an actual GPU- or queue-based target to scale against instead of the default CPU metric. Until that change happens, this exact failure — visible queuing and latency blowing past SLO while CPU graphs look fine and the HPA sits there doing nothing — is going to recur on every future traffic surge, because CPU utilization was never correlated with GPU-bound inference saturation to begin with.
questions.example: Under the surge, queue depth per replica climbs from 2 to 40 and p99 TTFT roughly triples, while CPU utilization stays near 15% the whole time; switching the HPA's target metric to queue depth (via a custom metrics adapter) would have triggered scale-out at the point queue depth first crossed a sane threshold, well before TTFT breached SLO.
commonMistakes: Treating low CPU utilization as evidence of genuine spare capacity for a GPU-bound workload
Assuming the HPA is malfunctioning rather than correctly scaling on the wrong metric
Not proposing a concrete alternative signal (queue depth, GPU utilization, latency) and how to wire it into the HPA
Forgetting that this requires a custom metrics API/adapter, not just changing a number in the HPA spec
Missing that this failure mode will recur on every future surge until the metric itself changes
keyPoints: CPU does little of the real work in GPU-bound inference; low CPU utilization under saturation is expected, not reassuring
The HPA is behaving correctly given its configured metric; the metric itself is the problem
Queue depth, GPU utilization, and latency-based signals all track actual inference load; CPU utilization does not
Implementing this requires the Kubernetes custom metrics API with an adapter (e.g. Prometheus Adapter)
Without this change, the same failure recurs on every future traffic surge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why CPU utilization stays low under GPU-bound saturation
Correctly identifies the metric choice, not the HPA mechanism, as the root cause
Proposes concrete, correct alternative signals
Names the mechanism (custom metrics API/adapter) needed to implement the fix

questions.title: Reproducibility Breaks Across Identical Distributed Runs
questions.prompt: Two runs of the same training job, launched with the identical seed, identical code, identical data, and identical FSDP configuration across 16 GPUs, produce slightly different loss curves after a few hundred steps, and the difference compounds over a longer run. The team assumed a fixed seed guaranteed identical runs. Explain the real sources of non-determinism at play and what, if anything, can actually be done about it.
questions.modelAnswer: A single torch.manual_seed call controls the pseudo-random number generator's sequence, but it does not make every operation in a distributed GPU training pipeline bit-for-bit deterministic, because several real sources of non-determinism exist independent of the seed: many CUDA kernels, especially for reductions, convolutions, and certain attention implementations, use algorithms whose exact floating-point summation order depends on runtime factors like available parallelism or thread scheduling, and floating-point addition is not associative, so a different summation order produces a genuinely different (though extremely close) numerical result even with identical inputs; this alone, with no other cause, is enough to make a GPU computation non-bit-reproducible run to run unless specific deterministic algorithm flags are set, and even then, deterministic modes often come with a real performance cost that production training rarely accepts. On top of kernel-level non-determinism, distributed collectives like all-reduce can themselves introduce run-to-run variation depending on the exact order floating-point values from different ranks are combined (ring all-reduce's summation order is a function of runtime network timing in some implementations), and DataLoader workers running in separate processes can introduce their own non-determinism in exactly which worker produces which batch first if the pipeline isn't carefully constructed to guarantee a fully deterministic batch order across multiple worker processes. Given this, the practical answer is that a fixed seed guarantees the same sequence of random numbers drawn, which is necessary but not sufficient for bit-for-bit reproducibility at scale; true determinism requires explicitly setting PyTorch's deterministic algorithm flags (torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)) and often CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG environment variables for cuBLAS determinism, accepting the throughput cost that comes with disabling certain fast, non-deterministic kernel implementations, and even then some distributed collective implementations may not offer a fully deterministic mode. For most large-scale training, the pragmatic stance is to treat exact bit-for-bit reproducibility as unattainable or prohibitively expensive, and instead focus reproducibility efforts on ensuring the same code, data, and config produce statistically equivalent results (same final loss within expected variance, same qualitative training dynamics) rather than promising an identical loss curve to the decimal, reserving true deterministic mode for narrow cases like debugging a specific numerical bug where bit-for-bit reproduction is genuinely needed for a short run.
questions.professionalAnswer: The team's assumption is a really common one, and it's wrong in a specific, well-understood way: a fixed seed controls the sequence of random numbers drawn, but it doesn't make the underlying GPU math itself bit-for-bit deterministic. A lot of CUDA kernels, especially reductions and some attention implementations, don't guarantee a fixed summation order, and floating-point addition isn't associative, so a different summation order gives you a genuinely different, if tiny, numerical result even with identical inputs — no seed controls that. Stack sixteen GPUs doing an all-reduce on top of that, where the order values get combined across ranks can itself vary run to run depending on runtime timing, and you've got a second independent source of drift. Small differences like that compound over hundreds of steps exactly the way the team is seeing. What can actually be done: PyTorch has torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) plus some CUBLAS environment variable settings that get you much closer to true bit-for-bit determinism, but it comes with a real throughput cost, since you're disabling some of the fastest, non-deterministic kernel implementations to get there — most production training jobs don't eat that cost. My honest recommendation for most teams is to stop chasing bit-for-bit reproducibility for full production runs and instead define reproducibility as 'same code, same data, same config produces statistically equivalent results' — same final loss within expected noise, same training dynamics — and reserve the expensive, fully deterministic mode for narrow debugging situations where you genuinely need to reproduce one specific run bit-for-bit over a short window.
questions.example: A reduction kernel summing a 4,096-element vector across different numbers of active thread blocks (which can itself depend on runtime scheduling) can produce a result differing in the last few bits of floating-point precision from run to run purely due to summation-order differences, even with the exact same input values.
commonMistakes: Assuming a fixed random seed is sufficient for bit-for-bit reproducibility in GPU/distributed training
Not recognizing floating-point non-associativity as a root cause of kernel-level non-determinism
Expecting torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) to be free, when it carries a real throughput cost
Treating any divergence in the loss curve as evidence of a real bug, rather than expected numerical noise
Not distinguishing bit-for-bit reproducibility from the more practical, achievable goal of statistically equivalent results
keyPoints: A fixed seed controls RNG draws but doesn't make GPU kernel math bit-for-bit deterministic
Floating-point non-associativity means summation-order differences produce genuinely different numerical results
Distributed collectives add their own run-to-run variation on top of kernel-level non-determinism
Deterministic algorithm flags exist but carry a real performance cost
The pragmatic goal for large-scale training is statistically equivalent results, not bit-for-bit reproducibility

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a fixed seed alone doesn't guarantee bit-for-bit determinism
Correctly identifies floating-point non-associativity as the mechanism
Identifies distributed collectives as an additional source of variation
Gives a sound, practical recommendation about what reproducibility goal is actually achievable

questions.title: A Resumed Checkpoint Trains Fine but Produces Subtly Wrong Behavior
questions.prompt: After a node failure, a training job resumes from its last checkpoint and training metrics (loss, gradient norm) look completely normal going forward, but a downstream evaluation several thousand steps later shows the model performing noticeably worse than models from equivalent points in previous, uninterrupted runs. No error occurred during the resume. Walk through what you'd investigate.
questions.modelAnswer: The fact that loss and gradient norm look normal rules out the most obvious failure modes (a corrupted weight tensor, a shape mismatch, a resume that silently dropped most of the model's parameters), since any of those would typically show up as an immediate, visible anomaly in those exact metrics, not a subtle downstream quality gap that only shows up in evaluation thousands of steps later. The leading hypothesis for a normal-looking loss curve but worse downstream quality is that something about the optimizer or scheduler state didn't resume correctly even though the model weights did, since optimizer state (Adam's running moment estimates) and the learning-rate scheduler's internal step counter can silently reset to a default or mismatched value without necessarily producing a visible loss spike, especially if the mismatch is partial (for example, only one of Adam's two moment buffers being dropped, or the LR scheduler resuming from step 0 instead of the correct global step, which would quietly run a different, effectively mis-timed learning-rate trajectory for the rest of training rather than an obviously broken one). A second, closely related hypothesis is that the data loader's resume point didn't correctly skip the examples already consumed before the failure, causing either a chunk of data to be seen twice (not catastrophic, but subtly biasing the effective data distribution for a portion of training) or a chunk to be skipped entirely, which again wouldn't show up as an anomalous loss value but could measurably affect final quality, especially if the skipped or duplicated data wasn't uniformly distributed across the dataset. The concrete investigation steps are: directly compare the resumed run's optimizer state (step count, and ideally a few actual values from Adam's moment buffers) against what the pre-failure checkpoint actually saved, to confirm the scheduler and optimizer state genuinely matches rather than silently defaulting; check the data loader/sampler's resume logic specifically, confirming it correctly tracked and skipped exactly the number of examples consumed before the failure rather than restarting the epoch or shard assignment from scratch; and compare the learning-rate value actually applied at each step immediately after resume against what the scheduler should have produced at that global step in an uninterrupted run, since a scheduler quietly resuming from the wrong step produces a wrong-but-plausible-looking LR trajectory that degrades final quality without ever producing an alarming-looking training curve.
questions.professionalAnswer: Normal loss and gradient norm is actually the thing that narrows this down for me — it rules out the loud failure modes, a corrupted weight tensor or a shape mismatch would show up immediately and obviously, not as a quiet downstream quality gap thousands of steps later. My leading theory is something in the optimizer or scheduler state didn't actually resume correctly even though the model weights did. Adam's moment buffers or the LR scheduler's step counter can silently reset or mismatch without producing a visible spike — if the scheduler resumed from step 0 instead of the correct global step, you get a different, quietly mis-timed learning-rate trajectory for the rest of training, which degrades final quality without ever looking alarming on a loss curve. Second theory, related: the data loader's resume point didn't correctly track exactly which examples were already consumed, so you either see a chunk of data twice or skip a chunk entirely — again, not something that shows up as an anomalous loss value, but something that can measurably bias final quality if that chunk wasn't uniformly representative. What I'd actually go check: pull the optimizer state right after resume and compare it against what the pre-failure checkpoint saved — confirm the step count and ideally some actual Adam moment values match, not just that no error was thrown. Separately, check the data loader/sampler's resume logic specifically, to confirm it skipped exactly the right number of already-consumed examples rather than restarting from the beginning of an epoch or shard. And I'd reconstruct what the LR should have been at each post-resume step in an uninterrupted run and compare it against what was actually applied — a scheduler quietly resuming from the wrong step produces a wrong, but perfectly plausible-looking, LR trajectory that's exactly the kind of thing that degrades quality without ever producing an obviously broken training curve.
questions.example: The checkpoint's manifest correctly restored model.state_dict() and optimizer.state_dict() but a bug in the resume script re-initialized the LR scheduler with last_epoch=-1 instead of passing the correct resumed step, causing the scheduler to restart its decay schedule from the beginning; the LR values produced were still plausible numbers, never triggering an anomaly, but the model trained the remainder of the run at a subtly wrong point in its intended decay curve.
commonMistakes: Assuming a normal-looking loss curve rules out any resume-related bug entirely
Checking only whether the resume completed without error, rather than whether the resumed state is actually correct
Not comparing the post-resume optimizer/scheduler state against the pre-failure checkpoint's saved values directly
Overlooking the data loader's resume point as a source of subtle quality degradation
Assuming any resume-related bug would necessarily produce a visible anomaly, when several plausible bugs specifically would not
keyPoints: A normal loss curve rules out loud failure modes (corrupted weights, shape mismatch) but not subtle state-resume bugs
A silently mis-resumed optimizer or scheduler state can produce a plausible-looking but wrong training trajectory
A data loader resume bug (duplicated or skipped examples) can bias effective data distribution without an anomalous metric
The investigation should directly compare post-resume state against the pre-failure checkpoint's saved values
Reconstructing the expected LR trajectory and comparing against what was actually applied can surface a scheduler resume bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about what a normal loss curve does and doesn't rule out
Proposes the optimizer/scheduler state mismatch hypothesis with concrete verification steps
Proposes the data loader resume-point hypothesis with concrete verification steps
Gives a coherent, well-justified overall investigation plan

questions.title: A torch.compile Model Intermittently Stalls for Several Seconds
questions.prompt: A training job wrapped with torch.compile runs at the expected speed most of the time, but every so often (roughly every few hundred steps, not on a fixed schedule) a single step takes 5-10 seconds instead of the usual 400ms, with no error raised and no OOM. The team assumed torch.compile's overhead was strictly a one-time cost at the start of training. Diagnose what's actually happening and how you'd confirm it.
questions.modelAnswer: torch.compile's compiled-kernel cache is keyed by the specific input shapes (and certain other properties) TorchDynamo observes on a given call; the common assumption that compilation is strictly a one-time, start-of-training cost holds only if every subsequent call presents exactly the shapes already compiled for. If the training pipeline occasionally produces a batch with a different shape than usual, most commonly a final, smaller batch at the end of an epoch (if drop_last isn't set), or a variable-length-sequence dataset where bucketing/padding occasionally produces an unusual sequence length, TorchDynamo detects that the new shape doesn't match any cached compiled graph and triggers a fresh recompilation for that shape, which involves re-running the TorchDynamo trace, AOTAutograd's backward-graph derivation, and TorchInductor's kernel compilation from scratch, an expensive process that can easily take several seconds, exactly matching the described symptom of an occasional, non-fixed-schedule 5-10 second stall with no error. This is checkable directly: setting TORCH_LOGS="recompiles" (or the equivalent compile-time logging flag) surfaces exactly which call triggered a recompilation and why, typically naming the specific shape or guard that failed to match the cached graph, which would confirm the hypothesis directly rather than leaving it as a guess. The fix is to eliminate the source of shape variation that's triggering repeated recompilation: setting drop_last=True on the DataLoader if the cause is an occasional smaller final batch, or padding/bucketing sequences to a small, fixed set of allowed lengths instead of truly variable lengths, so that TorchDynamo only ever sees a small, stable set of shapes across the entire run and compiles each one exactly once near the start of training rather than repeatedly over its lifetime.
questions.professionalAnswer: The 'one-time cost' assumption is the thing that's wrong here — it's one-time per distinct shape TorchDynamo sees, not one-time for the whole run. If the pipeline occasionally produces a batch with a different shape than what's already been compiled for — classically, a smaller final batch at the end of an epoch if drop_last isn't set, or a sequence-length dataset that isn't bucketed to a small fixed set of lengths — TorchDynamo has to recompile for that new shape on the spot, and that recompilation (tracing, deriving the backward graph, compiling kernels) is genuinely expensive, easily several seconds, which lines up exactly with the symptom described. I wouldn't just guess at this, though — I'd set TORCH_LOGS='recompiles' and actually watch which call triggers a recompile and why; it'll name the specific shape or guard mismatch directly, which turns this from a hypothesis into a confirmed cause. Once confirmed, the fix is removing the source of shape variation — drop_last=True if it's the final-batch case, or bucketing/padding sequence lengths to a small, fixed set of allowed sizes if it's a variable-length dataset — so TorchDynamo only ever sees a handful of distinct shapes across the whole run and compiles each one exactly once, genuinely near the start, instead of repeatedly recompiling at random points for the rest of training.
questions.example: A dataset with 50,000 examples and batch_size=64 produces 781 full batches of 64 and one final batch of 32 per epoch; without drop_last=True, every epoch's final step triggers a fresh recompilation for the 32-sized batch shape, producing exactly one unexplained multi-second stall per epoch.
commonMistakes: Assuming torch.compile's cost is strictly one-time for the entire run rather than per distinct shape encountered
Not using TORCH_LOGS='recompiles' to confirm the hypothesis directly before changing code
Fixing this by disabling torch.compile entirely instead of eliminating the specific shape-variation source
Not considering drop_last or sequence bucketing as the concrete, correct fixes
Assuming the stall is a hardware or network issue before checking compilation behavior specifically
keyPoints: torch.compile's compiled-kernel cache is keyed by input shape, not compiled once for the whole run
An occasional differently-shaped batch (e.g. a smaller final batch) triggers an expensive recompilation
TORCH_LOGS='recompiles' directly confirms which call triggered a recompile and why
The fix is eliminating shape variation (drop_last, sequence bucketing), not disabling compilation
This produces exactly the described non-fixed-schedule, multi-second stall pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies shape-triggered recompilation as the cause
Proposes a concrete, correct way to confirm the hypothesis (TORCH_LOGS)
Identifies a plausible concrete source of shape variation
Proposes the correct fix (drop_last / bucketing) rather than disabling compilation

questions.title: A Storage Migration Silently Halves Training Throughput
questions.prompt: Over a weekend, the platform team migrates training data from a parallel filesystem (FSx for Lustre) to a cheaper S3-backed object store to save cost, with no changes to the training code. On Monday, the same job runs at roughly half its previous steps/sec, with GPU utilization now visibly spiky rather than steady, but no errors anywhere in the logs. Diagnose what happened and what you'd check to confirm it.
questions.modelAnswer: The combination of halved throughput with no errors and a shift from steady to spiky GPU utilization is the classic signature of the data loader becoming the bottleneck: GPUs finish processing the current batch quickly and then sit idle waiting for the next one to arrive, producing a spiky rather than sustained utilization pattern, and the step-rate directly tracks however fast the (now slower) data pipeline can supply batches rather than how fast the GPUs can compute. The storage migration is the obvious and almost certainly correct suspect given it's the only thing that changed: object storage like S3 has meaningfully higher per-request latency than a parallel filesystem like FSx for Lustre, commonly tens of milliseconds per request versus a parallel filesystem's much lower latency, and while S3's aggregate throughput can scale well with enough parallel requests across many prefixes, a training job's DataLoader workers making many small, sequential or semi-sequential reads (especially for a sharded dataset not originally designed with S3's request-latency profile in mind) can be dominated by that per-request latency rather than by raw bandwidth, especially if the number of concurrent workers or the read pattern wasn't re-tuned for the new backend's different characteristics. The concrete confirmation steps: profile where time is actually going in the data-loading path specifically, for example by timing how long individual __getitem__ calls or object-fetch calls take now versus what they took against the old FSx-backed storage, and separately checking whether num_workers and the degree of read parallelism are high enough to amortize S3's per-request latency through concurrency, since the original num_workers setting was presumably tuned for FSx's very different latency profile and may be badly undersized for S3's higher-latency, more-parallelism-friendly access pattern. The fix, once confirmed, is either increasing num_workers/prefetch depth enough to hide S3's per-request latency behind enough concurrent in-flight requests, or re-introducing a caching/staging layer (such as using FSx for Lustre as a lazy-loading cache in front of S3, which is explicitly a supported pattern precisely for this kind of workload) rather than reading training data directly from S3 on every epoch.
questions.professionalAnswer: The spiky-instead-of-steady GPU utilization is the tell — that's the classic signature of the GPU finishing a batch and then just waiting for the next one, which means the data pipeline, not the model or the GPUs, is now the bottleneck. And since the storage migration is literally the only thing that changed over the weekend, that's where I'd focus immediately rather than looking at the training code at all. S3's per-request latency is just a different animal than a parallel filesystem's — tens of milliseconds per request is normal for S3, and while S3 scales well in aggregate with enough parallel requests, a DataLoader that was tuned for FSx's much lower per-request latency, with a num_workers setting sized for that old profile, can easily be latency-dominated now rather than bandwidth-dominated, especially if nobody re-tuned worker count or prefetch depth for the new backend. I'd confirm this directly by timing individual fetch calls in the data pipeline now versus what they used to take against FSx, and I'd check whether num_workers is actually high enough to keep enough requests in flight concurrently to hide S3's per-request latency behind parallelism. The fix, once that's confirmed, is either cranking up worker count and prefetch depth to amortize the latency through more concurrency, or — probably the better long-term answer — putting FSx back in front of S3 as a lazy-loading cache rather than reading training data straight from S3 every epoch, which is exactly the pattern FSx's S3 data-repository-association feature is built for.
questions.example: Individual object fetches that took roughly 1-2ms against FSx now take 15-25ms against S3; with num_workers unchanged from its FSx-tuned value, the data pipeline can no longer keep enough batches prefetched ahead of GPU consumption, and GPUs spend a growing fraction of each step idle waiting on the next batch.
commonMistakes: Investigating the model or training code first despite the storage migration being the only actual change
Not recognizing spiky GPU utilization as the specific signature of a data-pipeline bottleneck
Assuming S3's aggregate throughput capability means per-request latency can't be a bottleneck
Not checking whether num_workers/prefetch depth were re-tuned for the new storage backend's latency profile
Fixing this by reverting the migration entirely rather than considering a caching-layer approach that keeps the cost savings
keyPoints: Spiky GPU utilization with halved throughput and no errors points at the data pipeline becoming the bottleneck
The storage migration is the obvious suspect since it's the only actual change
S3's higher per-request latency can dominate over a DataLoader configuration tuned for a parallel filesystem's latency profile
Confirmation requires directly timing fetch calls and checking worker/prefetch concurrency against the new backend
A caching layer (e.g. FSx as a lazy-loading cache in front of S3) is a standard fix that preserves the cost savings

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reads the spiky-utilization symptom as a data-pipeline bottleneck
Correctly connects the storage migration's latency profile to the symptom
Proposes concrete confirmation steps (timing fetches, checking concurrency)
Proposes a sound fix that preserves the migration's cost intent where reasonable

questions.title: Deep Dive: A Multi-Day Pretraining Run Silently Diverges Partway Through
questions.prompt: You are the on-call infra engineer for a 256-GPU pretraining run expected to take 9 days. Around day 6, someone notices the training loss, which had been smoothly decreasing, has actually been slowly climbing for the past 14 hours — a gentle enough rise that no alert fired, since the team's only alerting rule was a hard threshold for loss exceeding a very high ceiling, not a trend-based check. No crash occurred; the job is still running, still checkpointing, and GPU utilization graphs look normal. Walk through a complete investigation: how you'd first confirm the problem is real and not a logging artifact, how you'd narrow down whether the cause lives in the GPU numerics layer, the data pipeline, or the distributed communication layer, what you'd actually do about the already-corrupted hours of training, and how you'd change the system so this class of failure is caught automatically next time.

deepDive.heading: Confirm the problem is real
deepDive.content: Before assuming the training loss metric itself is trustworthy, I'd check whether this is a genuine model-quality regression or a logging/metric-computation artifact. A loss value can drift due to a bug in how it's being logged or averaged (for example, a change in how often gradient accumulation boundaries align with logging boundaries, or a metric computed on a subtly different subset of ranks after a Worker rejoined post-preemption) without the model itself actually degrading. I'd pull an independent signal that doesn't share any code path with the training loss logger: run a quick held-out evaluation (perplexity on a fixed validation set) against the two most recent checkpoints, one from before the climb started and one from now. If eval perplexity also climbed correspondingly, the problem is real. If eval perplexity is flat while only the logged training loss climbed, I've just saved days of chasing a numerics bug that doesn't exist and should instead look at the logging/metric pipeline itself.

deepDive.heading: Narrow down: GPU numerics layer
deepDive.content: Assuming the regression is confirmed real, I'd check the numerics layer first since it's cheapest to inspect. I'd pull per-layer gradient-norm and activation-norm logs (if instrumented) for the 14-hour window and compare them against the same window's data from days 1-5. A numerics-layer cause would show a specific signature: one or a few layers' gradient or activation norms growing abnormally, possibly with GradScaler's skip-step counter (if using fp16) increasing in frequency over that window, consistent with the model's parameters having drifted into a numerically fragile region. I'd also check whether this coincides with any AMP/GradScaler scale-factor instability, or, if using bf16, whether a specific operation's precision characteristics could plausibly explain gradual degradation rather than a sharp spike.

deepDive.heading: Narrow down: data pipeline
deepDive.content: In parallel, I'd check whether the data pipeline is feeding something different starting around the point the climb began. This means checking whether a data shard boundary, a sharding reshuffle, or an upstream data refresh happened to land right around the 14-hour mark before the symptom appeared, and whether the actual token/example distribution in that window looks different from earlier windows (a quick check: log basic statistics -- sequence length distribution, vocabulary coverage -- per data shard and compare). A data-pipeline cause would show a specific, checkable correlation: the climb's onset lining up closely with a specific shard or data-source transition, rather than a smooth, cause-free drift.

deepDive.heading: Narrow down: distributed communication layer
deepDive.content: I'd also check whether this job experienced any Worker preemption, node replacement, or elastic re-formation event around the time the climb started, since a subtle correctness bug in how gradients are resharded or re-synchronized after a Worker rejoins (for example, a rank reconnecting with stale or mismatched optimizer state, or a partial, incorrectly-merged FSDP shard after a node swap) could introduce a persistent, compounding error that wouldn't crash anything but would quietly corrupt the effective gradient signal from that point forward. I'd check the job's own event log for any such re-formation event in the hours just before the climb began, since a correlated timing match here would be strong evidence this is the actual layer at fault, distinct from both the numerics and data hypotheses.

deepDive.heading: What the evidence actually shows and the remediation decision
deepDive.content: Suppose the investigation finds a Worker preemption and elastic re-formation event roughly 30 minutes before the climb's onset, and gradient-norm logs show one specific transformer block's gradients growing abnormally starting at almost the same time, with no suspicious data-shard transition in that window -- this points at the communication/re-formation layer as the trigger, likely a partially or incorrectly resynchronized optimizer or FSDP shard state after that specific Worker rejoined. Given that, the remediation decision is to roll back to the last checkpoint saved before that re-formation event, not to let the run continue, because the corruption is in persistent, compounding optimizer/gradient state, not a transient blip that would self-correct; continuing risks compounding the error further and wasting additional GPU-hours on a run that's already on a degraded trajectory. I'd resume from that last-known-good checkpoint, and specifically audit the elastic re-formation code path for how it resynchronizes FSDP shard state and optimizer state after a Worker rejoin, since that's now a confirmed, reproducible correctness risk rather than a theoretical one.

deepDive.heading: Fixing the systemic alerting gap
deepDive.content: The 14-hour undetected climb is itself a real failure independent of the root cause: a hard-threshold-only alert ('loss > X') is blind to exactly this class of problem, a slow, sustained trend well below any sane absolute ceiling. I'd add a trend-based alert, for example comparing a rolling window's average loss against the average from N hours earlier and firing if it's higher by more than a small margin sustained for a minimum duration (to avoid alerting on normal noise), alongside the existing hard-ceiling alert rather than replacing it. I'd also add an automated, periodic held-out evaluation (every few hours, not just at manually-triggered checkpoints) specifically so a logging-artifact-versus-real-regression question like the one in this investigation's first step can be answered automatically going forward, rather than requiring someone to manually notice a slow visual trend on a dashboard.

deepDive.heading: Operational follow-through
deepDive.content: Beyond the immediate fix and the alerting change, I'd write this up as a blameless postmortem naming the specific root cause (the elastic re-formation code path's shard resynchronization bug), the timeline (preemption event, climb onset, detection, rollback), and the two concrete action items (the code fix for the resync bug, and the new trend-based alert plus periodic automated eval), and I'd flag the resync code path for a targeted test that deliberately exercises a Worker preemption and re-formation mid-run in a smaller-scale staging job before the next large pretraining run, so this specific failure mode gets caught in staging rather than silently costing 14+ hours of GPU-time on a production run again.

commonMistakes: Assuming any one layer (numerics, data, or communication) is the cause without actually gathering evidence to distinguish them
Rolling back to before the divergence without first identifying what to actually fix, risking the exact same failure recurring
Treating 'no crash occurred' and 'GPU utilization looks normal' as evidence that nothing is wrong at the infrastructure layer
Fixing only the immediate run without changing the alerting strategy, leaving the same blind spot for the next long run
Confusing a genuinely corrupted internal state (that requires rollback) with a transient, self-recovering numerical blip (that wouldn't)
keyPoints: A slow, 14-hour climb with no alert firing reveals a real monitoring gap: threshold-based alerting missed a trend-based failure
Confirming the problem is real requires correlating the loss metric against an independent signal (eval perplexity, gradient norms) before trusting it
Each layer (numerics, data, communication) has a distinct, checkable signature that narrows the cause systematically
The remediation decision (roll back vs. continue) depends on whether the divergence corrupted persistent state (optimizer momentum) or was a transient, now-resolved cause
A durable fix requires both a point fix for this run and a systemic change (trend-based alerting) to catch the next occurrence automatically

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sound method for confirming the divergence is real, not a logging artifact
Proposes a systematic, evidence-based way to distinguish numerics, data, and communication causes
Makes and justifies a concrete remediation decision for the already-affected hours of training
Proposes a durable systemic fix (alerting/monitoring change) to catch this automatically next time

questions.title: Design a Feature Store and Model Registry for a Multi-Team ML Platform
questions.prompt: A company with five independent ML teams currently has each team building its own ad hoc feature-computation code and tracking models in spreadsheets. Design the shared feature store and model registry architecture you'd propose, covering online/offline separation, point-in-time correctness, and how multiple teams avoid colliding on feature definitions or model lifecycle state.
questions.modelAnswer: The feature store needs an offline store (backed by the existing data warehouse or lake, optimized for scanning history to build training sets) and a separate online store (a low-latency key-value store such as Redis or DynamoDB, holding only the latest value per entity for serving), connected by a materialization process that copies values from offline to online on a schedule matched to each feature's actual freshness requirement; this separation is non-negotiable because the two access patterns, historical scans versus single-key low-latency lookups, genuinely require different storage engines, and most feature-store training/serving-skew bugs come from teams maintaining two independent implementations of the same feature logic instead of sharing one FeatureView definition across both stores. Point-in-time correctness is enforced by requiring every training-set construction to go through a point-in-time join against the offline store, matching each historical label to the feature values as of that label's own event timestamp rather than the feature's current value, which is the mechanism that prevents future data from leaking into training sets; this should be a platform-enforced API, not a convention teams might forget, since the whole point is removing the chance for any team to accidentally bypass it. For five independent teams to share this without colliding, feature definitions need a namespacing and ownership model (each FeatureView tagged with an owning team and a version), and any change to an existing feature's logic should require either a new version/name rather than a silent redefinition, or an explicit migration path, so that a model trained against one definition of a feature doesn't silently start being served a differently-computed value without anyone noticing, a lineage failure the registry should make structurally hard to cause rather than merely discouraging through documentation. The model registry should track each model version's full lineage (the exact code commit, data snapshot, and feature versions used to produce it) and use a mutable alias system (champion/challenger-style pointers) rather than the older, deprecated stage-based lifecycle, since aliases are reassigned instantly without touching version history and avoid the structural flaw of a stage being a property of the version itself with no agreed cross-team meaning; each team should get its own registry namespace to avoid naming collisions, with a platform-level review gate only on registry-wide conventions (naming, required metadata), not on every individual promotion decision, which should remain within each team's own ownership.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start from the two-store split because it's non-negotiable, not a design choice up for debate — offline for history, online for fast single-key lookups, connected by materialization on a schedule matched to each feature's real freshness need. The thing I'd be most insistent on is making point-in-time correctness a platform API, not a convention — if it's just 'please remember to join on event timestamp,' someone eventually won't, and that's a silent data leak into a training set nobody will catch until the model underperforms in a way nobody can explain. For five teams sharing this, I'd give everyone their own namespace so nobody collides on names, and I'd make changing an existing feature's logic require a new version rather than a silent in-place redefinition — that's the one rule that prevents 'model A was trained on one definition of this feature and is now being served a different one' from ever happening invisibly. On the registry side, I'd push hard for aliases over the old stage-based lifecycle — champion/challenger pointers that move instantly without touching version history — and I'd keep promotion decisions within each team's own ownership, with the platform only enforcing shared conventions like required lineage metadata, not approving every individual promotion.
commonMistakes: Combining the offline and online store into one system instead of recognizing their genuinely different access patterns
Making point-in-time correctness a documented convention rather than a platform-enforced API
Allowing silent redefinition of an existing feature's logic without versioning, creating an undetectable lineage gap
Centralizing every team's model-promotion decision through one platform-level gate instead of per-team ownership with shared conventions
Not giving each team its own namespace, causing feature-name and model-name collisions across teams
keyPoints: Offline store for history, online store for low-latency serving, connected by scheduled materialization
Point-in-time joins must be a platform-enforced API, not a team convention, to prevent data leakage
Feature versioning/namespacing prevents silent redefinition and the resulting lineage failures
Model registry uses mutable aliases (champion/challenger) rather than the deprecated stage-based lifecycle
Per-team namespaces with shared platform conventions, not centralized approval of every promotion decision

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the offline/online split and materialization flow
Correctly enforces point-in-time correctness as a platform mechanism
Designs a sound multi-team namespacing/versioning scheme avoiding collisions
Designs a sound model registry lifecycle (aliases, lineage, ownership)

questions.title: Design an Inference-Serving Stack Under a Strict Cost and Latency Budget
questions.prompt: You need to serve a 13B-parameter chat model to roughly 10,000 concurrent users with a p99 TTFT SLO of 1.5 seconds, on a fixed monthly GPU budget that cannot grow. Design the serving architecture, including model/serving tool choice, batching strategy, autoscaling signal, and at least one cost-saving technique that doesn't compromise the latency SLO.
questions.modelAnswer: Given a strict, non-negotiable latency SLO and a fixed cost ceiling, the core serving engine should be vLLM (or a TensorRT-LLM-compiled engine if the team can invest the extra engineering time for maximum raw throughput per GPU), configured with continuous batching so GPU utilization stays high under the naturally bursty, variable-length request pattern of a chat workload, and PagedAttention-based KV-cache management to minimize memory waste and support shared-prefix reuse for common system prompts, which directly increases effective concurrent capacity per GPU without any additional hardware cost. Quantizing the model to a well-validated 8-bit or 4-bit scheme (e.g. via AWQ or GPTQ, with calibration data) is the first concrete cost-saving lever: it roughly halves or quarters the model's memory footprint, freeing substantially more room per GPU for KV cache (meaning more concurrent requests per GPU without more hardware) while typically costing only a small, measurable quality degradation that should be validated against task-specific evaluation, not just perplexity, before committing to it in production. Autoscaling should be driven by queue depth and/or measured TTFT percentiles per replica rather than CPU or even raw GPU utilization, since those are the signals that actually track whether the fleet is approaching the point where admission delay would start threatening the 1.5-second SLO; a reasonable design pre-computes, via load testing, the maximum sustainable concurrent request count per replica that keeps p99 TTFT under budget with some margin, and scales replica count to keep observed queue depth below the threshold that would start eating into that margin. For the fixed-budget constraint specifically, capacity planning should be done against measured peak concurrent load (not average), with a headroom factor covering unplanned spikes, and if budget is genuinely capped, the architecture should include a graceful-degradation path for load beyond the fleet's sized capacity, such as a request-admission queue with a bounded wait before returning a clear 'please retry' response, rather than letting p99 silently blow through SLO as load grows past what was budgeted for.
questions.professionalAnswer: With a fixed budget and a hard SLO, I'd start with vLLM for continuous batching and PagedAttention — that's free throughput per GPU before I spend a single extra dollar, since it keeps utilization high under chat's naturally bursty, variable-length traffic and lets common system-prompt prefixes share cache instead of duplicating it. Then I'd reach for quantization as the actual cost lever — AWQ or GPTQ to 8-bit or 4-bit, which roughly halves or quarters the weight footprint and hands that memory straight to the KV cache, meaning more concurrent users per GPU with zero new hardware. I'd validate that against task-specific eval, not just perplexity, before shipping it, because perplexity can look fine while a specific capability quietly degrades. For autoscaling I'd flatly refuse CPU-based signals — GPU-bound inference barely moves the CPU needle — and scale on queue depth or measured TTFT percentiles instead, with the trigger threshold set from actual load testing of what one replica can sustain while keeping p99 under 1.5 seconds. And because the budget is genuinely capped, I'd build in a graceful-degradation path — a bounded admission queue that returns a clear retry signal past capacity — rather than letting the SLO silently blow out when real demand exceeds what we sized for.
commonMistakes: Choosing a serving tool/batching strategy without connecting it to the specific stated TTFT SLO
Proposing CPU-utilization-based autoscaling for a GPU-bound serving workload
Treating quantization as purely a quality tradeoff without naming its direct, concrete effect on KV-cache capacity and cost
Not addressing what happens when real load exceeds the fixed budget's sized capacity (no graceful-degradation plan)
Sizing capacity against average rather than peak concurrent load
keyPoints: vLLM/TensorRT-LLM with continuous batching and PagedAttention for high utilization under bursty chat traffic
Quantization (AWQ/GPTQ) as a concrete, validated cost-saving lever that directly increases per-GPU concurrency
Autoscaling on queue depth or measured TTFT percentiles, not CPU/raw GPU utilization
Capacity sized against measured peak concurrent load with explicit headroom
A graceful-degradation path (bounded admission queue) for load beyond the fixed budget's sized capacity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Chooses and justifies a sound serving engine and batching/memory strategy
Proposes a concrete, validated cost-saving technique tied to the budget constraint
Designs correct, latency-aware autoscaling
Addresses graceful degradation when load exceeds the fixed capacity

questions.title: Design a Network Topology for a New 512-GPU Training Cluster
questions.prompt: You're specifying the leaf-spine network topology for a new 512-GPU training cluster (64 nodes, 8 GPUs each) that will primarily run large-scale pretraining jobs using FSDP and frequent all-reduce/all-gather collectives. Walk through your topology design choices: oversubscription ratio, blast radius considerations, and how you'd validate the fabric before trusting it with a production training run.
questions.modelAnswer: For a cluster whose workload is dominated by collective communication rather than, say, independent inference requests, the leaf switches connecting each rack's nodes should be sized with a 1:1 (non-blocking) oversubscription ratio between downlink capacity to the nodes and uplink capacity to the spine layer, since any oversubscription here directly throttles cross-rack all-reduce/all-gather traffic exactly when the cluster needs maximum bisection bandwidth, and training workloads, unlike many web-serving workloads, cannot tolerate that kind of throttling without directly inflating step time.
