Blast radius should be minimized at each layer of the topology: a single leaf-switch failure should take down no more than one rack's worth of nodes (typically 8-16 nodes depending on rack density), not a larger fraction of the cluster, and the spine layer should have enough redundant capacity that a single spine switch failure degrades available bisection bandwidth gracefully rather than partitioning the cluster; this argues for a spine layer with at least N+1 redundancy relative to the minimum number of spine switches the full bisection-bandwidth target requires, so a single spine failure is an absorbable capacity reduction rather than a correctness-threatening partition mid-job. Validation before trusting the fabric with a production run should proceed in the same cheapest-first order used for diagnosing problems: run nccl-tests' all_reduce_perf across the full 512-GPU topology and confirm busbw approaches the fabric's rated bandwidth (not just algbw, which systematically understates real throughput), check every node's InfiniBand (or equivalent) port counters via ibstat/perfquery for any node already showing elevated CRC/symbol errors or a degraded negotiated link speed before the cluster ever runs a real job, and run a smaller-scale shakedown training job (a subset of nodes, a short run) specifically to confirm gang scheduling, checkpointing, and elastic recovery all function correctly end to end, since topology and fabric validation alone doesn't confirm the orchestration layer above it is correctly wired for this specific cluster's configuration.
questions.professionalAnswer: For a cluster whose whole job is running collective-heavy FSDP training, I wouldn't even consider an oversubscribed leaf layer to save money — that's throttling exactly the traffic this cluster exists to move fast. 1:1 non-blocking leaf-to-spine is the right call here. On blast radius, I'd design so a leaf switch failure only ever takes out one rack's worth of nodes, and I'd put real redundancy in the spine layer — N+1 relative to what full bisection bandwidth needs — so a single spine failure degrades capacity gracefully instead of splitting the cluster mid-job, which would be a correctness problem, not just a slowdown. Before I'd trust this fabric with a real multi-week production run, I'd run nccl-tests' all_reduce_perf across the whole 512-GPU footprint and check busbw, not algbw, against the rated bandwidth — anything meaningfully short of that gets investigated before go-live, not after. I'd also pull ibstat and perfquery on every single node looking for pre-existing link degradation or climbing CRC errors, because catching that before the first real job is a lot cheaper than debugging it mid-run. And the last step, which people skip too often, is an actual shakedown job — a smaller subset of nodes, a short run — specifically to confirm gang scheduling, checkpointing, and elastic recovery are all correctly wired for this cluster's specific configuration, because a healthy fabric alone doesn't prove the orchestration layer on top of it is.
commonMistakes: Accepting an oversubscribed leaf layer for cost savings without recognizing the direct cost to collective-communication throughput
Not distinguishing leaf-switch blast radius (one rack) from spine-switch blast radius (potential cluster-wide partition)
Validating only with a synthetic nccl-tests run and never running an actual shakedown training job before production use
Comparing algbw instead of busbw against the fabric's rated bandwidth during validation
Designing for average-case bandwidth needs rather than the sustained, synchronous demands of collective operations
keyPoints: 1:1 (non-blocking) leaf oversubscription is appropriate given the collective-communication-heavy workload
Leaf-switch blast radius should be limited to one rack; spine layer needs redundancy to avoid cluster-wide partition risk
Validation proceeds cheapest-first: nccl-tests busbw, then per-node port-counter health checks, then an actual shakedown job
busbw, not algbw, is the correct metric to validate against rated bandwidth
Fabric validation alone doesn't confirm the orchestration layer (gang scheduling, checkpointing) is correctly wired

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly justifies a non-blocking leaf oversubscription ratio for this workload
Correctly reasons about blast radius at both the leaf and spine layers
Proposes a sound, correctly ordered fabric validation plan
Recognizes the need to validate the orchestration layer, not just the fabric

questions.title: Design a CI/CD/CT Pipeline for a Retraining-Heavy ML System
questions.prompt: Design a CI/CD/CT (continuous integration/delivery/training) pipeline for a fraud-detection model that needs to retrain weekly on fresh data, validate against the current production model before any promotion, and support fast rollback if a newly promoted model underperforms in production. Cover both the code-change trigger path and the data/schedule-trigger path.
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline needs to support two genuinely distinct triggers that both ultimately produce the same kind of artifact (a candidate model), and keeping them separable matters operationally: a code-change trigger (someone modifies the training or feature logic) should run CI (linting, unit tests, and a quick smoke-training run on a small data sample) before anything touches real data at scale, while the weekly schedule/data trigger runs the full continuous-training (CT) pipeline, pulling fresh data, retraining with pinned dependencies and a fixed seed for reproducibility, and logging the full run (code commit, data snapshot, config) to a tracking server. Both paths converge on the same validation gate before promotion: the candidate model is compared against the current production champion on a fixed, held-out evaluation set using the same metric the business actually cares about (not just an aggregate AUC, but slice-level performance on fraud sub-populations, since a fraud model regressing on one specific transaction pattern while improving in aggregate is exactly the kind of regression an aggregate-only gate would miss), and the gate should fail closed, meaning any validation failure blocks promotion and pages a human rather than defaulting to promote. Progressive delivery handles the deployment side: a passing candidate goes to shadow deployment first (receiving mirrored production traffic, predictions logged but not acted on, to catch infrastructure or latency issues with zero business risk), then a small canary slice of real, acted-on traffic, with automatic rollback wired to a hard threshold on both the fraud-detection business metric and basic infra metrics (error rate, latency) so a regression detected post-promotion reverts quickly without waiting for a human to notice. Fast rollback itself should be two-tiered: a model-level rollback via reassigning the registry's champion alias back to the previous version, which is nearly instant and requires no redeploy, as the first line of defense, with a full infrastructure rollback (reverting the serving deployment itself) reserved for the rarer case where the regression is actually in the serving code rather than the model.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep the two triggers genuinely separate rather than forcing them through one pipeline — a code change gets fast CI (lint, unit tests, a smoke-training run on a tiny data sample) before it's allowed anywhere near real data at scale, while the weekly schedule trigger runs the full CT pipeline with pinned dependencies, a fixed seed, and everything logged to a tracking server for reproducibility. Both paths land on the same validation gate though, and that gate is the part I'd be most careful about for a fraud model specifically — I wouldn't gate on aggregate AUC alone, because a model can improve in aggregate while quietly regressing on one specific fraud pattern, which is exactly the kind of thing that matters most and that an aggregate-only check would miss. The gate fails closed — any failure blocks promotion and pages someone, it never defaults to 'promote anyway.' On the deployment side, a passing candidate goes to shadow first to catch infra issues with zero business risk, then a small canary slice of real traffic with automatic rollback wired to both the fraud business metric and basic infra metrics, continuously evaluated, not just checked at the end of a soak window. And I'd build rollback in two tiers — flipping the registry's champion alias back is the fast, near-instant first move, with a full infrastructure rollback reserved for the rarer case where the actual regression turns out to be in the serving code, not the model.
commonMistakes: Coupling the code-change CI path with the full-scale weekly retraining pipeline instead of keeping them separable
Gating promotion only on an aggregate metric, missing slice-level regressions on specific sub-populations
Designing the validation gate to default to promote on an ambiguous or missing result instead of failing closed
Skipping shadow deployment and canary, going straight from validation to full production traffic
Not distinguishing fast model-level rollback (alias reassignment) from slower infrastructure-level rollback
keyPoints: Code-change CI and scheduled/data-triggered CT are separate paths that converge on the same validation gate
Validation must check slice-level performance, not just an aggregate metric, especially for fraud
The validation gate fails closed and pages a human rather than defaulting to promote
Progressive delivery (shadow then canary) with automatic rollback on business and infra metrics
Two-tiered rollback: fast alias reassignment first, full infrastructure rollback only if needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates and connects the code-change and data/schedule trigger paths
Designs a validation gate with slice-level checks and fail-closed behavior
Designs a sound progressive-delivery deployment strategy
Designs a correct, two-tiered rollback strategy

questions.title: Design an Observability and SLO Stack for a Multi-Service ML Platform
questions.prompt: Design the observability stack for an ML platform with three layers that each need their own health signal: the feature pipeline, the model-serving fleet, and the model's actual prediction quality in production. Define an SLI/SLO for each layer, and explain how you'd avoid alert fatigue while still catching a real regression in any of the three.
questions.modelAnswer: Each of the three layers needs a distinct SLI because they fail in genuinely different ways and conflating them into one dashboard metric would hide which layer actually broke. The feature pipeline's SLI should be freshness and completeness (e.g., 'percentage of expected materialization jobs completing within their expected window, with row-count sanity checks against the prior run'), with an SLO like 99% of materialization windows met within a defined staleness bound, since a feature pipeline can 'succeed' in an infrastructure sense while quietly producing stale or incomplete data, a failure mode infra-only alerting wouldn't catch. The model-serving fleet's SLI should be request-level: p99 latency and error rate, with an SLO such as p99 latency under a defined threshold and error rate under a small percentage over a rolling window, which is standard infra observability and should alert on sustained SLO burn rate rather than raw instantaneous metric wobble, since model-serving metrics are naturally noisy and alerting on every blip causes exactly the alert fatigue the design needs to avoid. The model's prediction-quality SLI is the hardest and most distinct: it requires either near-real-time ground truth (rare) or a proxy such as prediction-distribution drift (PSI against a training-time baseline) and slice-level business-metric tracking, with an SLO framed around sustained drift beyond a threshold or a sustained business-metric decline, explicitly on a trend-detecting basis rather than a hard instantaneous ceiling, since the earlier reasoning about silent quality degradation shows that a slow decline is exactly the failure mode a threshold-only alert misses. To avoid alert fatigue while catching real regressions across all three: alert on sustained burn rate against each SLO's error budget rather than raw metric values, give fast-burn alerts (threatening to exhaust the budget within hours) a paging severity and slow-burn alerts (threatening to exhaust it over days) a ticket-only severity, and periodically audit alerts that haven't led to any real human action in 90 days for demotion or deletion rather than letting them accumulate as background noise that trains the on-call team to ignore pages.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd refuse to use one blended health metric across all three layers, because they fail in completely different ways and a blended metric just hides which one actually broke. For the feature pipeline, I'd define the SLI around freshness and completeness, not just 'did the job exit zero' — a materialization job can succeed in every infrastructure sense while quietly producing stale or incomplete data, and that's a real failure mode a plain job-success check won't catch. The serving fleet gets the standard treatment — p99 latency and error rate — but I'd alert on sustained SLO burn rate, not raw metric wobble, because model-serving metrics are naturally noisy and alerting on every blip is exactly how you train your on-call team to ignore pages. Prediction quality is the hardest one — I'd use PSI-style drift detection against the training-time baseline plus slice-level business-metric tracking, and critically, I'd make that SLO trend-based, not a hard ceiling, because the whole failure mode worth worrying about here is a slow decline that never crosses an absolute threshold. Across all three, I'd give fast-burn alerts a paging severity and slow-burn alerts a ticket-only severity, and I'd actually go back every quarter and kill or demote any alert that hasn't driven a real human action in 90 days — an alert nobody acts on isn't neutral, it's actively making the real pages easier to miss.
commonMistakes: Using one blended dashboard metric across all three layers instead of distinct, layer-appropriate SLIs
Defining the feature pipeline's health purely as 'job succeeded' without a freshness/completeness check
Alerting on raw instantaneous metric values instead of sustained SLO burn rate, causing alert fatigue
Using only a hard threshold for prediction-quality monitoring, missing a slow, trend-based decline
Giving every alert the same paging severity regardless of fast-burn versus slow-burn urgency
keyPoints: Each layer (feature pipeline, serving fleet, prediction quality) needs a distinct, appropriately-defined SLI
Feature pipeline SLI should check freshness/completeness, not just job success
Serving fleet SLO is standard latency/error-rate, alerted on sustained burn rate, not raw wobble
Prediction-quality SLI needs a trend-based (drift, sustained decline) definition, not just a hard ceiling
Fast-burn vs. slow-burn severity differentiation plus periodic alert audits prevent fatigue

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Defines a distinct, appropriate SLI/SLO for each of the three layers
Correctly designs burn-rate-based alerting rather than raw-threshold alerting
Addresses the trend-based nature of prediction-quality monitoring specifically
Proposes a concrete alert-fatigue mitigation strategy

questions.title: Design a Multi-Tenant GPU Sharing Strategy for a Shared Research Cluster
questions.prompt: A 64-GPU research cluster is shared by multiple small teams running interactive notebooks, short experiments, and occasional larger training jobs. GPUs sit idle much of the time (interactive work is bursty) but teams frequently complain they can't get a GPU when they need one. Design a GPU-sharing strategy, weighing MIG, time-slicing, and bin-packing/scheduling policy, and explain the tradeoffs of your choice.
questions.modelAnswer: The core tension is that interactive, bursty workloads want instant access to a small amount of GPU capacity, while occasional larger training jobs want full, unshared GPUs, and a single sharing mechanism applied uniformly to all workloads on the cluster will serve one of these well at the expense of the other. The right design uses different mechanisms for different workload classes rather than one blanket policy: for interactive notebook and small-experiment workloads, MIG partitioning on a subset of the fleet (say, a third of the nodes) provides genuine hardware-level isolation, carving each physical GPU into several smaller, fully isolated instances so multiple users can each get guaranteed, isolated capacity without one user's runaway notebook process starving another's, which solves the 'I just need a GPU to debug something small' complaint directly; time-slicing is explicitly the wrong tool here because it provides no memory isolation, meaning one user's memory-hungry process can still degrade or crash another's workload sharing the same time-sliced GPU, which would reproduce the exact unpredictability driving the complaints in the first place. For the occasional larger training jobs, a separate pool of full, unpartitioned GPUs (the remaining two-thirds of the fleet) should be governed by a fair-share queue (via Slurm or a Kubernetes-based batch scheduler with queue weighting) rather than MIG or time-slicing, since those jobs genuinely need a full GPU's memory and compute, and queueing with a reasonable wait-time SLA is a better fit than trying to fractionally share capacity a large job can't actually use in fractions. Addressing the idle-but-unavailable complaint specifically requires combining this mechanism split with a usage policy: a maximum per-user/per-team GPU-hours cap or a preemption policy that allows a queued large job to reclaim idle capacity from a long-running-but-low-utilization interactive session after a grace period, since mechanism alone (MIG for interactive, queue for large jobs) doesn't prevent a single team from monopolizing the large-job pool indefinitely if nothing caps or preempts that usage.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't apply one sharing mechanism to the whole fleet, because interactive work and large training jobs actually want opposite things — interactive wants instant, small, isolated access, large jobs want a full, unshared GPU. So I'd split the fleet: a third of the nodes get MIG-partitioned for interactive and small-experiment use, because MIG gives real hardware-level isolation, which matters a lot when the complaint is 'someone else's runaway notebook killed my session.' I'd explicitly rule out time-slicing for that workload class, because it gives you zero memory isolation — one user's memory-hungry process can still crash or starve someone else sharing the same time-sliced GPU, which just reproduces the exact unpredictability driving the complaints in the first place. The remaining two-thirds stay as full, unpartitioned GPUs behind a fair-share queue — Slurm or a Kubernetes batch scheduler with queue weighting — because large jobs genuinely need the whole GPU and queueing with a reasonable wait-time expectation is a better fit than trying to fraction out capacity they can't use in fractions anyway. But I wouldn't stop at the mechanism split — I'd add a usage policy too, either a per-team GPU-hour cap or a preemption rule letting a queued large job reclaim idle capacity from a long-running, low-utilization session after a grace period, because without that, nothing stops one team from just sitting on the large-job pool indefinitely even when they're barely using it.
commonMistakes: Applying one sharing mechanism (MIG or time-slicing) uniformly to both interactive and large-job workloads
Choosing time-slicing for the interactive workload class despite its lack of memory isolation being the exact problem driving complaints
Designing the mechanism split without also addressing usage policy (caps, preemption) for the idle-but-monopolized complaint
Not recognizing that large training jobs genuinely need full, unpartitioned GPUs rather than any fractional-sharing scheme
Treating MIG's hardware-level isolation and time-slicing's lack of isolation as interchangeable tradeoffs
keyPoints: Interactive/bursty and large-training workload classes need genuinely different sharing mechanisms, not one blanket policy
MIG's hardware-level isolation fits interactive workloads; time-slicing's lack of memory isolation makes it the wrong fit there
Large training jobs need full, unpartitioned GPUs governed by a fair-share queue, not fractional sharing
Mechanism choice alone doesn't solve monopolization; a usage policy (caps/preemption) is also needed
The design should split the fleet into pools matched to each workload class's actual needs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the needs of interactive vs. large-job workload classes
Correctly justifies MIG over time-slicing for the interactive workload class
Designs a sound queueing/scheduling approach for the large-job pool
Addresses usage-policy (caps/preemption) needed beyond mechanism choice alone

questions.title: Design Data Storage and Pipeline Tiering for Large-Scale Training Data
questions.prompt: Design the storage architecture for a training dataset that is 50TB today and growing, read repeatedly across many training runs by a 64-node GPU cluster. Walk through your choice between object storage, block storage, and a parallel filesystem, and how data flows from the system of record to the GPUs during training.
questions.modelAnswer: Block storage (such as cloud EBS-style volumes) should be ruled out immediately as the shared training-data store, since it attaches to a single instance and cannot be concurrently read by 64 nodes at once; its role, if any, is local scratch space on individual nodes, not the shared dataset. Object storage (S3 or equivalent) is the right choice as the durable system of record: it's cheap at this scale, scales well in aggregate throughput with enough parallel requests across prefixes, and is the natural landing place for a growing 50TB dataset that needs durability and doesn't need per-request latency in the single-digit milliseconds. However, reading training data directly from object storage on every epoch, for every node, risks being limited by object storage's higher per-request latency (commonly tens of milliseconds) rather than by aggregate bandwidth, especially for a data-loading pattern involving many smaller reads across a sharded dataset; the architecture should therefore layer a parallel filesystem (such as FSx for Lustre) between object storage and the training cluster, configured with a data-repository association that lazily loads objects from S3 on first read and then serves subsequent reads (across the same or later training runs) from the parallel filesystem's own fast, concurrent, low-latency storage, which directly addresses the 'read repeatedly across many runs' part of the requirement, since after the first pass the data is effectively cached at the parallel-filesystem tier for all later runs. For sharding specifically, the number of shards should significantly outnumber the total concurrent reader count across the cluster (64 nodes times however many DataLoader workers per node), so no worker ever waits on a shard someone else is still streaming through, and shard sizes should be tuned so that per-shard read time is long enough to amortize one open/seek overhead but short enough that an uneven shard-to-worker assignment doesn't create a meaningfully unbalanced load. The overall flow is: system of record in S3, lazily and persistently cached in FSx for Lustre for fast, concurrent, low-latency access, read by DataLoader workers in large enough shard counts to avoid worker starvation, with local NVMe on each node reserved for OS scratch and any node-local temp files, never as the shared dataset store itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: Block storage is out immediately — it attaches to one instance, it simply can't be the thing 64 nodes read concurrently, so its only role here is local scratch on individual nodes, not the shared dataset. Object storage is the right system of record for a growing 50TB dataset — cheap, durable, scales in aggregate throughput — but I wouldn't have every node read straight from it on every single epoch, because per-request latency on object storage, tens of milliseconds typically, can dominate over raw bandwidth for a sharded dataset with a lot of smaller reads. I'd put a parallel filesystem like FSx for Lustre in front of it with a lazy-loading data-repository association — first read pulls from S3, every read after that, across this run and future runs, hits FSx's own fast, concurrent, low-latency storage instead, which directly answers the 'read repeatedly across many runs' part of this. On sharding, I'd make sure shard count significantly outnumbers total concurrent readers — 64 nodes times however many workers per node — so nobody's ever stuck waiting on a shard someone else is still streaming through. And local NVMe stays scoped to OS scratch and temp files on each node — it's never the shared dataset store across all 64 nodes, that's not what it's for.
commonMistakes: Proposing block storage as the shared dataset store, missing that it can't serve 64 nodes concurrently
Reading training data directly from object storage on every run without a caching layer, risking per-request-latency-bound throughput
Not sizing shard count significantly above the total concurrent reader count, risking worker starvation on a popular shard
Proposing local NVMe as the shared dataset store across all 64 nodes instead of OS scratch/temp use only
Not addressing the 'read repeatedly across many runs' requirement specifically, missing the caching benefit a parallel filesystem provides
keyPoints: Block storage is ruled out as the shared store; it attaches to a single instance only
Object storage (S3) is the correct durable system of record for a growing 50TB dataset
A parallel filesystem (e.g. FSx for Lustre) with a lazy-loading S3 data-repository association provides fast, concurrent, low-latency access and effectively caches repeated reads
Shard count should significantly exceed total concurrent reader count to avoid worker starvation
Local NVMe is for OS scratch/temp use, never the shared dataset store across all nodes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rules out block storage and justifies object storage as the system of record
Correctly proposes a parallel-filesystem caching layer and explains its latency/throughput benefit
Correctly reasons about shard count relative to concurrent readers
Correctly scopes local NVMe's role

questions.title: Design a Cost-Attribution System for a Shared Multi-Tenant Training Cluster
questions.prompt: A shared 256-GPU cluster serves three teams. Finance wants an accurate monthly cost breakdown per team, including a fair allocation of shared overhead (control plane, monitoring, idle capacity). Design the cost-attribution architecture and explain how you'd handle the two hardest cases: a team whose GPUs sit at 40% utilization while fully reserved, and genuinely shared infrastructure that no single team's usage cleanly explains.
questions.modelAnswer: The foundation for per-team attribution should be namespace- or label-based: if each team's workloads run in their own Kubernetes namespace (or equivalent logical boundary), a cost-attribution tool like Kubecost can attribute GPU cost to whichever pods actually request GPU resources, proportional to each pod's GPU request, close to automatically, since the namespace boundary already matches the attribution boundary that matters; this should be the primary mechanism rather than something built from scratch, since this is a well-understood, largely solved problem for container-based GPU workloads. The first hard case, a team's GPUs sitting at 40% utilization while fully reserved, should not be hidden or smoothed over in the reporting; the design should surface both the team's full reserved cost (what they're actually being charged, since the GPUs are reserved for their exclusive use regardless of utilization) and their utilization rate as a separate, visible metric, because conflating the two (for example, only charging for 'GPU-hours actually used') would remove the economic signal that utilization matters at all, while reporting only the reserved cost with no utilization visibility hides a genuine cost problem from the team that's actually responsible for it; the right answer is transparency on both numbers together, letting the team (and finance) see that they're paying full reserved price for a GPU pool running at less than half capacity, which is itself the lever that should drive that team toward either releasing excess reservation or improving their own job packing. The second hard case, genuinely shared infrastructure (the Kubernetes control plane, cluster-wide monitoring, shared networking) that no single team's usage cleanly explains, should be allocated proportionally to each team's measured resource consumption (their share of total GPU-hours, or total compute-hours, consumed over the billing period) rather than split evenly across teams regardless of usage, since an even split systematically overcharges a lighter user and undercharges a heavy one for infrastructure whose actual cost driver is usage volume; this proportional allocation should be computed and reported transparently (showing both the team's direct cost and their proportional share of shared overhead as separate line items) so teams can see exactly what's driving each part of their bill rather than receiving one opaque total.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't build this from scratch — namespace or label-based attribution with something like Kubecost gets you most of the way for free, since GPU cost attributes to whichever pods actually request it, proportional to each pod's request, and that boundary already matches what finance cares about if each team runs in its own namespace. The 40%-utilization-at-full-reservation case is the one I'd be most deliberate about — I wouldn't hide it by only reporting the reserved cost, and I wouldn't hide the cost either by only reporting utilization. I'd show both numbers side by side: this is what you're actually being charged for your reservation, and here's how much of it you're using — because that's the exact signal that should push the team toward either releasing capacity or packing jobs better, and burying either number removes that incentive. For genuinely shared infrastructure — control plane, cluster-wide monitoring — I'd allocate it proportional to each team's measured usage, their share of total GPU-hours over the period, rather than splitting it evenly, because an even split quietly overcharges whoever uses the cluster lightly and undercharges the heavy user. And I'd present all of this as separate line items — direct cost, proportional shared overhead, utilization — rather than one number, so teams can actually see what's driving their bill instead of just trusting a total.
commonMistakes: Building a custom cost-attribution system from scratch instead of using established namespace/label-based tooling
Hiding the utilization-versus-reserved-cost gap instead of surfacing both numbers transparently
Splitting shared overhead evenly across teams regardless of actual usage volume
Presenting cost attribution as one opaque total rather than separate, legible line items (direct cost vs. shared overhead share)
Treating low utilization at full reservation as purely a reporting problem rather than connecting it to an actual incentive lever
keyPoints: Namespace/label-based attribution (e.g. Kubecost) is the correct foundation, not a custom-built system
Low utilization at full reservation should be surfaced transparently as both reserved cost and a separate utilization metric
Genuinely shared overhead should be allocated proportionally to measured usage, not split evenly
Transparent, itemized reporting (direct cost vs. shared-overhead share) is preferable to one opaque total
Cost attribution should create a visible incentive signal, not just a billing exercise

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sound namespace/label-based attribution foundation
Correctly handles the low-utilization-at-full-reservation case with transparency
Correctly allocates genuinely shared overhead proportional to usage
Proposes clear, itemized reporting rather than an opaque total

questions.title: Design a KV-Cache-Aware Serving Architecture for Multiple Concurrent Models
questions.prompt: You need to serve four different fine-tuned variants of the same 7B base model to different internal teams, all with similar latency requirements, on a fixed pool of GPUs. Design a serving architecture that avoids loading four full 7B models into memory, and explain the memory and cost tradeoffs of your approach versus the naive one.
questions.modelAnswer: The naive approach, loading each of the four fine-tuned variants as a completely separate full model, requires four times the weight memory of a single 7B model, which both wastes GPU memory that could otherwise go toward KV cache (directly limiting concurrent request capacity) and wastes GPU count if each variant needs its own dedicated replica, since four separate full models likely can't all fit on the GPUs a single properly-sized base-model deployment would use. If the four variants were produced via LoRA fine-tuning (a common and often preferred approach specifically because of this serving-cost benefit) rather than full fine-tuning, the correct architecture loads the shared 7B base model's weights exactly once, and represents each variant as a small LoRA adapter, often tens to a few hundred megabytes rather than many gigabytes, applied on top of the shared base weights at inference time; a serving framework with multi-adapter support (vLLM has this capability) can then route each incoming request to the correct adapter dynamically, swapping which small adapter is applied per request while the large base weights stay resident and shared across all four teams' traffic. This dramatically changes the memory math: instead of 4x the base model's weight memory, you pay roughly 1x the base weight memory plus four small adapter footprints, freeing the memory difference for KV cache, which directly increases how many concurrent requests across all four teams the same GPU pool can serve; it also means the four teams' traffic can share one pool of replicas rather than needing four dedicated pools, improving utilization since each team's individual traffic pattern is bursty and the shared pool absorbs that burstiness better than four separately-sized small pools would. The tradeoff to be explicit about: this only works if the variants were (or can be) produced via LoRA rather than full fine-tuning, since full fine-tuning genuinely produces four distinct full-weight models with no shared-base-plus-small-delta structure to exploit; if full fine-tuning is a hard requirement for quality reasons, the architecture reverts to needing separate models, and the cost-saving story here doesn't apply.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first question would actually be whether these four variants were produced via LoRA or full fine-tuning, because that decides everything else. If they're full fine-tunes, there's genuinely no shared structure to exploit and you're stuck with four separate models. But if LoRA's on the table, the architecture changes completely: load the shared 7B base weights exactly once, and represent each team's variant as a small adapter on top — tens to a couple hundred megabytes instead of many gigabytes per variant. vLLM supports multi-adapter serving, so one pool of replicas can route each request to the right adapter dynamically while the big base weights stay resident and shared across all four teams' traffic. The payoff is real: instead of paying for 4x the base model's weight memory, you're paying roughly 1x plus four small adapters, and all that freed memory goes straight into KV cache, which directly means more concurrent capacity for everyone, on the same GPU pool, with one shared replica pool absorbing each team's individual burstiness better than four separately-sized small pools would. I'd flag clearly, though, that this entire story depends on LoRA — if quality requirements genuinely force full fine-tuning, this design doesn't apply and we're back to separate deployments.
commonMistakes: Proposing four separate full-model deployments without considering whether LoRA fine-tuning is applicable
Not quantifying the actual memory-saving mechanism (base weights once, small adapters per variant)
Missing that freed weight memory directly translates into more KV cache and therefore more concurrent capacity
Not addressing the real constraint that this approach requires LoRA (or similar parameter-efficient) fine-tuning, not full fine-tuning
Proposing four separate replica pools instead of one shared pool serving all four variants' traffic
keyPoints: Naive four-separate-models approach wastes memory (4x weights) and likely GPU count
LoRA-based variants let the base model's weights load once, shared across all variants
A multi-adapter-capable serving framework (e.g. vLLM) routes requests to the correct small adapter dynamically
Freed weight memory directly increases available KV cache and concurrent capacity
This architecture specifically requires the variants to be LoRA (not fully) fine-tuned

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the naive approach's memory/cost waste
Correctly designs the shared-base-plus-LoRA-adapter architecture
Correctly connects freed memory to increased KV cache / concurrency
Explicitly names the LoRA-vs-full-fine-tuning constraint on this approach

questions.title: Design a Gang-Scheduling and Queue-Fairness System for a Multi-Team Training Cluster
questions.prompt: A 128-GPU cluster is shared by two teams submitting large, multi-node distributed training jobs. Each job needs all its pods scheduled simultaneously (gang scheduling), and the cluster needs to avoid both deadlock between two large jobs competing for the same capacity and one team monopolizing the cluster indefinitely. Design the scheduling system.
questions.modelAnswer: Plain Kubernetes scheduling is insufficient here because it has no concept of a group of pods that must all be schedulable together, so the foundation needs a gang-scheduling layer such as Volcano, with every multi-node job submitted as a PodGroup whose minMember exactly matches the job's total pod count, ensuring Volcano holds every pod of a job Pending until the entire group can be placed simultaneously, which is the mechanism that directly prevents a job from partially launching and then hanging forever waiting on ranks that were never scheduled. Avoiding deadlock between two large jobs each holding partial capacity while waiting for more (the classic failure mode when two gang-scheduled jobs are allowed to both partially reserve resources at once) requires that the gang-scheduling guarantee itself (via minMember as above) ensures no job holds any resources at all until it can be fully scheduled, which structurally prevents the deadlock scenario, since a job either gets 100% of what it needs atomically or holds nothing, with no partial-reservation state for two jobs to deadlock over. Fairness between the two teams is handled by Volcano's queue mechanism: each team gets its own Queue object with a weight proportional to its agreed share of the cluster (for example, equal weights if the teams are meant to have equal claim) and a capability cap as an absolute ceiling so neither team can be starved entirely nor can either team exceed its fair allocation even during periods when the other team isn't submitting jobs, preventing the monopolization concern directly. For the case where the cluster has free capacity beyond what currently-queued jobs need, the design should still respect queue weighting rather than first-come-first-served, so that if both teams submit large jobs simultaneously, each gets scheduled proportional to its queue weight rather than whichever team happened to submit microseconds earlier claiming everything; and for capacity that genuinely sits idle because no job from either team currently needs it, the scheduler should allow either team to use it up to their capability ceiling, giving back the freed capacity the moment the other team's queued job can use its fair share again.
questions.professionalAnswer: Plain Kubernetes scheduling doesn't have a concept of 'this group of pods all gets scheduled together or none of them do,' so the foundation has to be a gang-scheduling layer — Volcano, with every multi-node job submitted as a PodGroup whose minMember exactly matches its real pod count, so a job can't partially launch and then sit there hanging on ranks that were never actually scheduled. The deadlock concern basically disappears once that all-or-nothing guarantee is real — a job holds either 100% of what it needs or nothing at all, so there's no partial-reservation state for two large jobs to deadlock over in the first place. For fairness between the two teams, I'd give each one its own Queue with a weight reflecting their agreed share — equal if that's the deal — plus a capability cap as a hard ceiling, so neither team can be starved during a burst and neither can quietly eat more than their fair share even when the other team's queue is empty. If both teams submit large jobs at the same moment, I'd want the scheduler respecting queue weight, not first-come-first-served, so it isn't just whoever happened to submit a few milliseconds earlier that gets everything. And for capacity that's genuinely idle because nobody's queued for it, either team should be able to use it up to their capability ceiling, giving it back the moment the other team actually needs their fair share again.
commonMistakes: Using plain Kubernetes scheduling without a gang-scheduling layer, allowing partial launches to hang
Setting minMember lower than the job's actual pod count, which doesn't provide a real all-or-nothing guarantee
Not recognizing that the all-or-nothing gang guarantee itself is what structurally prevents the partial-reservation deadlock
Using only weight without a capability cap, allowing one team to starve the other during a burst
Allowing first-come-first-served scheduling when both teams submit simultaneously instead of respecting queue weighting
keyPoints: Volcano (or equivalent) PodGroups with minMember matching the full job size provide the gang-scheduling guarantee
The all-or-nothing guarantee itself (no partial reservation) structurally prevents deadlock between two large jobs
Per-team Queue objects with weight (relative share) and capability (absolute cap) provide fairness
Weight and capability together prevent both starvation and monopolization
Idle capacity beyond current queued need can be used up to a team's capability ceiling, released when needed elsewhere

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the gang-scheduling mechanism (PodGroup/minMember)
Correctly explains how the all-or-nothing guarantee prevents deadlock
Correctly designs the per-team queue weight/capability fairness mechanism
Addresses how idle capacity is shared without undermining fairness

questions.title: Design an Audit-Logging and Lineage System for a Regulated ML Platform
questions.prompt: A fintech company's credit-risk model is subject to regulatory audit. Design the audit-logging and lineage architecture that lets you answer, for any model version ever in production, exactly what data, code, and configuration produced it, who approved its promotion, and when it was live, with the log itself being tamper-resistant.
questions.modelAnswer: The system needs to capture four distinct lineage links, each closed by its own mechanism rather than one generic log: the data link is closed by attaching a structured, versioned dataset reference to every training run (for example via a data-versioning tool's content hash, logged against the run), the code link is closed by capturing the exact git commit SHA the training code ran at as a tag on the run, the run-to-model-version link is closed by the model registry storing the run ID on every model version it creates, and the 'who approved this and when did it go live' link is closed by deployment and approval metadata that's separate from the training run itself, since nothing upstream of an actual promotion decision can know who approved it or when it started serving traffic. All four of these should write into an append-only, write-once audit log, not just the system's regular operational database, because a log that could be quietly edited after an incident or audit request provides no real guarantee to a regulator; concretely this means using a dedicated audit-log service or object storage with object-lock/WORM (write-once-read-many) enabled specifically for the audit trail, separate from the mutable operational metadata stores the platform uses day to day, so that even someone with full admin access to the operational systems cannot retroactively alter the audit record. Answering 'what produced this model version' for an audit request then becomes a lookup chain: start from the model version in the registry, follow its stored run ID to the training run's logged commit SHA and data-version tag, and separately pull the deployment/promotion audit log entries for that version to get who approved it and the exact timestamps it was live, with every step of that chain backed by the tamper-resistant log rather than by institutional memory or a spreadsheet. Retention needs to match the regulatory window (often several years for financial models), which argues for tiering: the small, audit-critical artifacts (manifests, approval records, model cards) stay in the tamper-resistant log for the full regulatory window regardless of a cost-driven lifecycle policy, while large artifacts (the actual model binary, full training datasets) can follow a more cost-optimized storage tier as long as their content hashes remain in the permanent audit log, preserving the ability to verify integrity even if the full binary has been moved to cheaper, slower storage.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd break this into four distinct links rather than trying to solve it with one generic log, because each one needs a different mechanism: the data link closed by a versioned dataset hash logged against the run, the code link closed by the exact git commit SHA tagged on the run, the run-to-model-version link closed by the registry storing the run ID on every version it creates, and the approval/deployment link — who signed off and when it actually went live — closed separately, since nothing about the training run itself can know that. The part I'd push hardest on is that none of this goes into the regular operational database — it goes into a dedicated, write-once audit log, object storage with object-lock or an equivalent WORM mechanism, specifically so that even someone with full admin access to our normal systems can't quietly edit the record after the fact. A regulator isn't going to accept 'trust us, nobody touched it' if the log was technically editable. Answering an audit request then becomes a traceable chain — start at the model version in the registry, follow its run ID back to the commit and data hash, pull the separate approval log for who signed off and when — every link backed by the tamper-resistant log, not institutional memory. And on retention, I'd tier it: small audit-critical records — manifests, approvals, model cards — stay in the WORM store for the full regulatory window no matter what, while the big stuff, model binaries and full datasets, can move to cheaper storage as long as their hashes stay permanently in the audit log so we can still verify integrity later.
commonMistakes: Logging lineage into the regular, mutable operational database instead of a dedicated tamper-resistant audit log
Missing the deployment/approval metadata link, which can't be reconstructed from the training run alone
Not distinguishing which four lineage links need to be captured and by what specific mechanism each
Applying a single, cost-driven retention policy to both large binaries and small audit-critical records, risking auditability
Not considering that even admin-level operational access must not be able to retroactively alter the audit record
keyPoints: Four distinct lineage links (data, code, run-to-version, deployment/approval) each need their own capture mechanism
The audit trail must be append-only/write-once (WORM), separate from mutable operational metadata
A 'what produced this model' audit request is answered via a lookup chain through the registry and audit log
Retention should tier: small audit-critical records kept for the full regulatory window, large binaries on a cost-optimized tier with their hashes preserved permanently
Even full admin access to operational systems must not be able to alter the tamper-resistant audit record

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and designs mechanisms for all four lineage links
Correctly designs a tamper-resistant, append-only audit log distinct from operational storage
Describes a coherent lookup chain for answering an audit request
Addresses retention tiering appropriate to regulatory requirements

questions.title: Design an Autoscaling Policy for a Bursty, GPU-Bound Serving Workload
questions.prompt: A customer-facing chat feature has highly bursty traffic: near-zero load most of the day, with sharp 10x spikes during specific hours. GPU-based inference replicas take roughly 3 minutes to become ready (model load time). Design the autoscaling policy so the fleet is both cost-efficient during quiet periods and doesn't violate the latency SLO during a spike.
questions.modelAnswer: The 3-minute replica-readiness time is the central constraint this design has to work around, because a purely reactive autoscaler that waits for queue depth or latency to breach a threshold before scaling out will, by the time new replicas are actually ready 3 minutes later, have already let the SLO violation persist for the entire readiness window, which for a sharp 10x spike could mean minutes of degraded or failed requests before relief arrives. The design should combine three mechanisms rather than relying on reactive autoscaling alone: first, a warm minimum replica count sized to comfortably handle baseline (non-spike) traffic with some margin, so the fleet never scales all the way down to zero or near-zero even during quiet periods, trading a modest, bounded idle cost for eliminating the worst-case 'scaling from zero' readiness delay; second, if the spike timing is predictable (a known daily pattern, e.g. a lunch-hour or evening peak), a scheduled pre-scaling action that proactively adds replicas a few minutes before the historically known spike window begins, converting a reactive scramble into a planned, already-ready capacity increase, which directly neutralizes the 3-minute readiness constraint for predictable spikes; third, reactive autoscaling on queue depth (not CPU, which is useless for GPU-bound inference) as the fallback for genuinely unpredictable spikes, with the autoscaler's target threshold set conservatively low, triggering scale-out well before queue depth would actually threaten the SLO, specifically to buy enough lead time to absorb the 3-minute readiness delay without breaching the SLO in the interim. Cost-efficiency during quiet periods comes from the warm-minimum being sized to baseline, not peak, load, and from scaling back down (on a slower, more conservative schedule than scale-out, to avoid flapping) once a spike passes; the combination of predictable pre-scaling for known patterns and conservative-threshold reactive scaling for the unpredictable remainder is what actually respects the 3-minute constraint, rather than either pure reactive scaling (too slow) or massively over-provisioning a large static fleet at all times (defeats the cost-efficiency goal).
questions.professionalAnswer: The 3-minute load time is the whole design problem here — if I rely purely on reactive scaling, by the time new replicas are actually ready, a sharp 10x spike has already been violating SLO for however long it takes to notice plus 3 minutes, which for a chat feature is a real chunk of degraded user experience. So I wouldn't lean on reactive scaling alone. First move: a warm minimum replica count sized to baseline traffic with some margin, so we never scale to zero and never face the worst-case cold-start delay — yes, that costs something during quiet hours, but it's a small, bounded cost against a much worse tail risk. Second move, if the spike timing is at all predictable — a known daily pattern — I'd add scheduled pre-scaling that adds replicas a few minutes ahead of the historical spike window, which basically neutralizes the 3-minute constraint for anything we can see coming. Third, for the genuinely unpredictable remainder, reactive autoscaling on queue depth, never CPU, with the trigger threshold set deliberately conservative — triggering well before queue depth would actually threaten the SLO, specifically to buy enough lead time to absorb that 3-minute delay. And I'd make scale-down slower and more conservative than scale-out, so we're not flapping replicas up and down right after a spike passes.
commonMistakes: Proposing pure reactive autoscaling without addressing the 3-minute readiness delay's effect on SLO during a sharp spike
Scaling the warm-minimum replica count to zero during quiet periods, reintroducing the worst-case cold-start delay
Not proposing scheduled pre-scaling for predictable spike patterns, missing a direct mitigation for the readiness constraint
Setting the reactive-scaling threshold too close to the SLO breach point, leaving no lead time to absorb the readiness delay
Scaling down as aggressively/quickly as scaling up, risking flapping right after a spike passes
keyPoints: The 3-minute replica-readiness time is the central constraint the policy must be designed around
A warm minimum replica count avoids the worst-case cold-start delay during quiet periods at a bounded cost
Scheduled pre-scaling for predictable spike timing directly neutralizes the readiness constraint for known patterns
Reactive autoscaling on queue depth (not CPU) handles unpredictable spikes, with a conservative threshold providing lead time
Scale-down should be slower/more conservative than scale-out to avoid flapping

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the replica-readiness time as the central design constraint
Proposes a sound warm-minimum strategy balancing cost and readiness
Proposes scheduled pre-scaling for predictable spikes
Proposes correct reactive autoscaling (queue-depth-based, conservative threshold) for the unpredictable remainder

questions.title: Design a Progressive-Delivery and Rollback Strategy for Retrained Models
questions.prompt: Design the end-to-end progressive-delivery pipeline a newly retrained model goes through before serving 100% of production traffic, for a product-recommendation model where a bad model degrades revenue but doesn't cause outright errors or crashes. Explain why shadow deployment alone is insufficient here and how your canary stages and rollback triggers address that gap.
questions.modelAnswer: Shadow deployment, where the candidate model receives mirrored traffic and its predictions are logged but never acted on or shown to users, is valuable for catching infrastructure problems (latency, crashes, obviously malformed output) with zero business risk, but it has a specific, important blind spot for a recommendation model: you cannot know whether a discarded recommendation would have actually been clicked, purchased, or otherwise driven the business outcome the model exists to improve, because it was never actually shown to a real user and acted on; a recommendation model can pass shadow deployment cleanly (no crashes, no malformed output, plausible-looking predictions) while still being measurably worse at the actual job of driving engagement or revenue, a gap shadow deployment structurally cannot detect. The pipeline needs real, acted-on traffic to measure the thing that actually matters, which is exactly what canary stages provide: a small initial canary (e.g., 1-5% of real traffic) held for long enough to get a statistically meaningful read on the actual business metric (click-through rate, conversion, revenue per session) the retraining was meant to improve, not just infrastructure health, followed by progressively larger stages (10%, 50%) each held long enough to rule out short-term novelty effects or day-of-week confounds before committing more traffic. The rollback trigger set needs to include the business metric explicitly, not just infra signals: a hard threshold such as 'click-through rate or revenue per session falling more than X% below the champion's baseline, sustained over a minimum window to filter out normal noise' should trigger an automatic rollback (reverting the registry alias back to the champion) at any stage, continuously evaluated rather than only checked at stage boundaries, since the entire reason to run this progressively rather than cutting over immediately is to limit how much real revenue is ever exposed to a model that turns out to be worse, which only works if detection and rollback both happen quickly once a stage's traffic reveals the problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: Shadow deployment is great for catching the stuff that would obviously break — crashes, malformed output, latency blowups — with zero business risk, but it has a blind spot that matters a lot for a recommendation model specifically: a discarded prediction was never actually shown to a real user, so you can't tell whether it would have been clicked or converted. A recommendation model can sail through shadow deployment looking completely fine while still being measurably worse at the actual job it exists to do, and shadow deployment structurally can't catch that because it never lets the prediction touch reality. That's exactly why I'd insist on real canary stages with real, acted-on traffic — starting small, 1-5%, held long enough to get an actual statistically meaningful read on click-through or revenue per session, then 10%, then 50%, each stage held long enough to rule out novelty effects or day-of-week noise before I'd trust it. And the rollback trigger has to include the business metric explicitly, not just error rate and latency — something like 'CTR or revenue per session drops more than X% below the champion's baseline, sustained over a minimum window to filter noise' — evaluated continuously throughout every stage, not just checked when a stage ends. The entire reason to do this progressively instead of cutting over all at once is to cap how much real revenue is ever exposed to a worse model, and that promise only holds if detection and rollback are both fast enough to matter.
commonMistakes: Treating shadow deployment as sufficient validation for a model whose failure mode is business-metric degradation, not crashes or errors
Gating canary promotion only on infrastructure metrics (latency, error rate) without a business-metric threshold
Not holding canary stages long enough to distinguish a real effect from short-term novelty or day-of-week noise
Checking rollback conditions only at stage boundaries instead of continuously throughout each stage
Not explaining why shadow deployment's blind spot specifically applies to this kind of model (no crashes, just quieter quality degradation)
keyPoints: Shadow deployment catches infra/crash issues but cannot measure real, acted-on business impact
A recommendation model can pass shadow deployment cleanly while still underperforming at its actual job
Canary stages with real, acted-on traffic are required to measure the business metric that actually matters
Stages need to be held long enough to rule out novelty and day-of-week confounds
Rollback triggers must include the business metric explicitly and evaluate continuously, not just at stage boundaries

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains shadow deployment's specific blind spot for this model type
Designs a sound progressive canary staging structure
Designs a rollback trigger that explicitly includes the business metric
Addresses continuous evaluation and confound-avoidance (novelty, day-of-week)

questions.title: Deep Dive: End-to-End Fault-Tolerant Infrastructure for a 500+ GPU Pretraining Run
questions.prompt: Design the complete infrastructure for a from-scratch pretraining run on 512 H100 GPUs (64 nodes, 8 GPUs each) expected to run continuously for roughly 5 weeks. Cover the compute/network topology, the checkpointing and failure-recovery strategy, the orchestration layer, data pipeline, observability/alerting, and cost attribution, and explain how all of these pieces work together when a node actually fails mid-run.

deepDive.heading: Clarify requirements and constraints
deepDive.content: 512 H100s across 64 nodes running continuously for 5 weeks means the design has to assume failures will happen, not treat them as an edge case: at even a conservative 2% annualized per-GPU failure rate, 512 GPUs running continuously compounds to a real, expected number of individual GPU failures over a 5-week window, the same compounding logic as a birthday-paradox argument across many independent draws. The design's success criterion isn't 'avoid failure,' it's 'bound how much work any single failure destroys, and recover automatically within a predictable, acceptable amount of time.'

deepDive.heading: Network and compute topology
deepDive.content: Leaf switches use a 1:1 non-blocking oversubscription ratio, since this workload's step time is dominated by collective communication (FSDP's all-gather/reduce-scatter) and any leaf-layer oversubscription directly throttles exactly the traffic the cluster depends on. Blast radius is minimized per layer: a leaf-switch failure takes down one rack (8-16 nodes), not more, and the spine layer carries enough redundant capacity that a single spine failure degrades available bisection bandwidth rather than partitioning the cluster mid-job. Before trusting the fabric with the real run, nccl-tests' all_reduce_perf across the full 512-GPU topology should show busbw approaching the fabric's rated bandwidth, and every node's InfiniBand port counters should be checked for pre-existing degradation via ibstat/perfquery.

deepDive.heading: Checkpointing and the failure-recovery strategy
deepDive.content: Checkpoint interval should be derived from the actual expected-failure-rate math, not picked arbitrarily: given roughly 10 expected GPU failures across 512 GPUs over a year (at 2% annualized), scaled to the 5-week run's duration, gives an expected failure count for this specific run, and checkpoint frequency should be set so the expected lost work between checkpoints (failure rate times checkpoint interval) stays within an acceptable fraction of total GPU-hours, balanced against the real overhead checkpointing itself imposes on step time. Checkpoints are saved via torch.distributed.checkpoint (DCP), with each rank saving only its own shard in parallel rather than gathering onto one rank, which would turn every checkpoint into a single-rank serialization bottleneck. The master/rank-0 role (anchoring rendezvous and driving checkpoint writes) runs on on-demand, non-preemptible capacity specifically because losing it loses the job's entire coordination point, not just one worker's GPUs; Worker replicas can run on a more cost-optimized mix since they're individually replaceable.

deepDive.heading: Orchestration: gang scheduling and elastic recovery together
deepDive.content: Initial launch uses gang scheduling (a Volcano PodGroup with minMember matching the full 64-node pod count) so the job never partially launches and hangs waiting for ranks that were never scheduled. Once running, mid-run node failures are handled by torch.distributed.elastic with an --nnodes range whose floor is set well above a handful of nodes (training at a tiny fraction of capacity isn't worth continuing versus waiting for repaired capacity) and a --max-restarts budget sized to the run's realistic failure rate over its full 5-week duration, not an arbitrary small number. A failed node is cordoned and drained (kubectl cordon then drain) so repair/diagnostics can proceed without workload dependency, while the elastic agent re-forms the group around the remaining healthy nodes and resumes from the last checkpoint.

deepDive.heading: Data pipeline integration
deepDive.content: Training data lives in object storage as the system of record, fronted by a parallel filesystem (e.g. FSx for Lustre) with a lazy-loading data-repository association, so repeated reads across the run's duration hit fast, low-latency storage rather than being bound by object storage's per-request latency. Shard count is set to significantly outnumber the total concurrent reader count (64 nodes times workers per node) so no worker stalls waiting on a shard someone else is still streaming. This matters for fault tolerance specifically because a starved data pipeline produces a symptom (idle-looking GPUs, stalled-looking progress) that's easy to misdiagnose as a hang or a hardware failure if the data pipeline isn't monitored as its own layer.

deepDive.heading: Observability and alerting
deepDive.content: Alerting needs both a hard-threshold tier (loss exceeding an absolute ceiling, NCCL watchdog timeouts, node Xid errors) that pages immediately, and a trend-based tier (loss or gradient norm trending upward over a sustained multi-hour window well below any hard ceiling, or DCGM showing high GPU_UTIL with low PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE sustained over time) that catches the class of failure a threshold alone misses: a slow divergence or a silently communication-bound stretch that never crashes anything. A periodic, automated held-out evaluation (not just the training loss curve) gives an independent signal to confirm whether a suspicious trend is a real model-quality issue or a logging artifact.

deepDive.heading: What happens when a node actually fails mid-run
deepDive.content: A node's GPU logs an Xid hardware error; NCCL's watchdog on the ranks waiting for that node's participation in the current collective times out after its configured window, converting what would otherwise be a silent hang into an explicit error. The elastic agent detects the failed rank, and because --max-restarts hasn't been exhausted, the job re-forms its process group around the remaining nodes rather than failing outright. The node is cordoned and drained for hardware diagnostics. Training resumes from the last DCP checkpoint, losing at most the work done since that checkpoint, which the checkpoint-interval math was specifically sized to bound. Cost attribution for the failed node's downtime and the brief re-formation pause is captured in the namespace-based cost tooling as reduced utilization for that period, visible rather than hidden in the team's cost report, and the incident is logged as a data point feeding back into whether the checkpoint interval or the max-restarts budget needs adjustment for future runs of similar scale and duration.

commonMistakes: Designing checkpoint frequency without doing the actual failure-rate math to justify the chosen interval
Keeping the rendezvous/coordination role on preemptible or equally-replaceable capacity as ordinary workers
Treating gang scheduling and elastic recovery as redundant instead of serving genuinely different moments (initial launch vs. mid-run recovery)
Designing alerting only on hard thresholds, missing the slow-divergence and silently-stalled-run failure modes
Not considering data-loader throughput and storage tiering as part of the fault-tolerance story, when a starved GPU looks like a hang but isn't one
keyPoints: A non-blocking leaf/spine topology sized for the collective-communication-heavy workload, with blast radius minimized per layer
Checkpoint interval derived from an actual GPU failure-rate estimate, trading checkpoint overhead against expected lost work
Gang scheduling (all-or-nothing) for initial launch, elastic training (torch.distributed.elastic) for mid-run recovery after a node failure
Rank-0/coordination role kept off preemptible capacity; workers can be more cost-optimized
Alerting needs both hard thresholds and trend-based checks to catch stalls and slow divergence, not just crashes
Cost attribution via namespace/label-based tooling, with utilization made visible alongside reserved cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound network topology appropriate to the communication-heavy workload
Designs a checkpointing strategy grounded in an actual failure-rate argument
Designs a coherent orchestration layer covering both initial gang-scheduled launch and mid-run elastic recovery
Designs observability/alerting that catches both hard failures and silent degradation
Addresses data pipeline and cost attribution as integrated parts of the design, not afterthoughts

questions.title: Leading the Response to a Major Training Outage
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you led (or would lead) the response to a serious production incident on infrastructure you were responsible for — a training cluster outage, a serving fleet degradation, or similar. Walk through how you organized the response, communicated status, and what you did in the postmortem.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer establishes a concrete incident (what broke, what the blast radius was, how it was detected), then walks through a clear incident-command structure: naming a single person (often the answerer) as incident lead responsible for coordinating rather than personally fixing everything, assigning specific investigation threads to specific people rather than everyone looking at everything at once, and establishing a regular communication cadence to stakeholders (a status update every 15-30 minutes during an active incident, even if the update is 'still investigating, next update at X time') so people aren't left guessing. The answer should include a concrete mitigation decision made under uncertainty, such as rolling back a change, failing over to a backup, or accepting a temporary capacity reduction to stop the bleeding before the root cause was fully understood, and should explain the reasoning behind choosing mitigation-first over root-cause-first when the two are in tension. The postmortem description should be blameless by name, focusing on what the system or process allowed to happen rather than who made a mistake, and should produce concrete, assigned action items (not vague 'improve monitoring' but a specific alert, test, or process change with an owner and a deadline) that the answerer can describe following up on later, demonstrating the postmortem actually changed something rather than being a ritual.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through a specific incident rather than speaking in generalities, because that's what actually demonstrates how I handle this. The structure I always fall back on is: name one incident lead immediately, even if it's informal, so there's one person coordinating instead of five people independently debugging the same problem. I split investigation into specific threads and assign them to specific people, and I set a communication cadence up front — even 'still investigating, next update in 20 minutes' is better than silence, because silence is what makes stakeholders start escalating on their own. The part I'd emphasize most is being willing to mitigate before I fully understand the root cause — rolling back a recent change, or accepting a temporary capacity hit, to stop the bleeding, rather than insisting on a complete diagnosis before acting, because in a live incident the cost of continued impact usually outweighs the cost of a slightly premature mitigation. For the postmortem, I keep it genuinely blameless — the conversation is about what the system or the process allowed to happen, not who made the call — and I push for specific, owned action items with real deadlines, not vague aspirations, because a postmortem that doesn't produce something concrete and assigned is just a meeting that happened.
commonMistakes: Describing only what broke without explaining how the response was actually organized
Not naming a clear incident-command structure or communication cadence
Insisting on full root-cause understanding before taking any mitigating action
Describing a postmortem that assigns blame rather than focusing on systemic causes
Giving vague, unassigned follow-up items ('we should monitor this better') instead of concrete, owned ones
keyPoints: Clear incident-command structure: one lead, specific threads assigned to specific people
A defined communication cadence that prevents stakeholders from being left guessing
Willingness to mitigate before fully understanding root cause when impact is ongoing
A genuinely blameless postmortem focused on systemic, not individual, causes
Concrete, owned, deadline-bound action items that demonstrate real follow-through

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a specific, credible incident with real detail
Demonstrates a clear incident-command and communication structure
Explains a sound mitigation-vs-root-cause tradeoff decision
Describes a genuinely blameless postmortem with concrete action items

questions.title: Making a Capacity-Planning Tradeoff Under a Fixed GPU Budget
questions.prompt: Describe a time you had to make a real tradeoff decision when GPU or infrastructure budget was fixed and couldn't grow, but multiple legitimate needs (more training capacity, more serving capacity, reliability headroom) were all competing for it. How did you decide, and how did you communicate the tradeoff to the people whose request you said no to?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names the specific competing needs and the actual numbers involved (how much capacity each need required, how much was available), rather than speaking abstractly about 'competing priorities.' It should describe a real decision framework used to adjudicate, such as ranking needs by business impact and reversibility (is this need something that can wait a sprint without real cost, or does delay itself have a compounding cost), rather than simply picking whichever team asked loudest or escalated highest. The answer should be honest about the real cost of the choice made, acknowledging that saying no to one legitimate need has a real downside for that team rather than presenting the decision as costless or obviously correct in hindsight. The communication part matters as much as the decision itself: the answer should describe explaining the reasoning (not just the decision) to the team that didn't get what they asked for, ideally with a concrete plan for when their need would be revisited (a specific future point, like the next budget cycle or a named capacity-freeing event) rather than an open-ended 'maybe later,' since a team that understands why and when is far more likely to accept the decision than a team that just hears 'no.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give a specific example with real numbers, because 'competing priorities' without specifics doesn't actually show how I think through a hard tradeoff. The framework I use is ranking by business impact and reversibility — is this something that can genuinely wait without compounding cost, or does delaying it itself get more expensive the longer it waits — rather than just going with whoever escalated the loudest, which is a trap that's easy to fall into under pressure. I'd be honest that whatever I chose had a real cost for the team that didn't get what they asked for — I wouldn't pretend the decision was costless or obviously correct, because it usually isn't, it's just the least-bad option given a real constraint. The part I think matters most, though, is how I communicated it — I didn't just deliver a no, I walked through the actual reasoning with the team that didn't get their ask, and I gave them something concrete: a specific point, not a vague 'later,' at which their need would get revisited, whether that's the next budget cycle or a named event like a planned capacity expansion. A team that understands why and has an actual date to look forward to handles a no a lot better than a team that just hears 'not now' with nothing else attached.
commonMistakes: Describing the tradeoff abstractly without naming specific competing needs or real numbers
Presenting the decision as obviously correct or costless, ignoring the real downside to the team that didn't get what they needed
Deciding based on who escalated loudest rather than a consistent decision framework
Not describing how the decision was actually communicated to the team that didn't get their request
Giving an open-ended 'maybe later' instead of a concrete point at which the need would be revisited
keyPoints: Names specific competing needs and real numbers, not abstractions
Uses a consistent decision framework (business impact, reversibility) rather than reacting to escalation
Is honest about the real cost of the decision to the team that didn't get what they needed
Explains the reasoning, not just the decision, to the affected team
Provides a concrete point at which the deferred need will be revisited

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives a specific, concrete example with real tradeoffs
Describes a consistent, defensible decision framework
Is honest about the real cost of the decision
Describes clear, constructive communication to the affected team

questions.title: Getting Skeptical ML Researchers to Adopt Platform Tooling
questions.prompt: Describe a time you needed to get a team of ML researchers or scientists to adopt a platform tool or standard (a feature store, a tracking system, a checkpointing convention) that they were skeptical of, viewing it as unnecessary overhead on top of their existing workflow. How did you approach winning them over, and what did you do differently for a researcher who remained unconvinced?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer avoids treating 'researchers are skeptical of process' as an obstacle to overcome through authority or mandate, and instead describes understanding the actual cost the researchers perceive the new tool imposing on their workflow, since skepticism toward platform tooling is usually a rational response to a real, if sometimes overstated, perceived cost (learning curve, slower iteration, loss of control) rather than mere resistance to change for its own sake. The approach should involve demonstrating value concretely rather than asserting it: picking a specific, real pain point the researchers already have (for example, a lost experiment result, or an inability to reproduce a result from three weeks ago) and showing how the new tool directly solves that exact pain point for them, ideally by solving it for one real researcher's actual problem first rather than rolling out broadly and asking everyone to adopt it on faith.
